acts 19 repaired as 41 entries, one per verse — no pericopes, because every verse in this chapter draws distinct comment from six to nine witnesses, and grouping would have discarded material rather than avoided templating. Only v.7 (134 usable source words) took the thin exemption. The old prose carried all three audit defect shapes: 'The witnesses note' opening most sentences, the full KJV verse in quotes at the head of all 41 entries, and near-duplicate sentences restating the same point three or four times. Regenerated throughout. John Chrysostom's homily block sits under key 8 but covers vv.8-40, and is drawn on at vv.8, 13, 21, 24, 25 and 26.

FIXED 2026-08-15: the pericope expansion-ratio defect reported from the numbers 32 run is closed. QA.span_source_text/span_keys now answer 'what does this entry stand on', and both synthesis-fidelity.py and the expansion that backfill-synthesis-qa.py stamps go through them, so a ranged entry is measured against the union of its span — the same span the thin exemption has always summed. All 50 ranged entries in the four chapters that use ranges (genesis/24, joshua/17, numbers/7, numbers/32) were re-stamped with the real numbers using the new --keep-generated flag, which preserves qa.generated because a re-measurement is not a regeneration. 14 false STRETCH flags disappeared (worst: numbers 7:6 at a reported 24.12x, really 0.93x; genesis 24:39 at 24.68x, really 1.4x; numbers 32:18 at 9.6x, really 1.09x). Verified against a HEAD worktree that non-ranged chapters are byte-identical. Left deliberately unchanged: the ratio still counts scrape residue in the denominator, which understates it on chrome-heavy verses but errs toward not flagging.

Five Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks in this chapter are foreign-passage material and were declared as excluded_voices on the entries covering them: v.5 holds JFB on the proclamation of the divine name at Exodus 34; vv.11, 17, 23 and 29 all carry the same fragment about bowing the head to royalty in the East. JFB is named nowhere in the prose. The v.47 blob also ends in a long tail of StudyLight page chrome (CSS, inline JS, the site's book_data array), which inflates its measured source from ~350 real words to 1,379.

Ellicott's note on leviticus 11:44 introduces the quotation 'be ye holy, for I am holy' with 'the Apostle Paul uses the same admonition' and then quotes 1 Peter 1:15-16. The attribution is wrong in the source. The prose credits it to 'the apostle' without naming him and anchors 1 Peter 1:15, so the error is neither reproduced nor silently corrected into a claim Ellicott did not make.

Three ENTITIES flags judged false positives, all spelling normalisations of the source's older forms: v.17 'Delft' (Gill writes 'the city of Delf in Holland'), v.20 'Libyans' (Wesley writes 'Lybians'), v.29 'Nile' (Keil and Delitzsch write 'lacerta Nilotica', which the matcher does not expand). None introduces a claim absent from the source.

One entry self-graded B: the 39-40 pericope, whose closing paragraph sets the chapter's remediable ceremonial defilement (water, a broken pot, the coming of evening) against the excision reserved for deliberate contempt. The excision itself is Ellicott's and Wesley's point on this verse; the contrast drawn across the whole chapter is the summary's own framing. Every other entry graded A. Expansion ratios run 0.14x-0.73x — heavy distillation throughout, since the sources here are enormous and largely natural-history digression.

leviticus 11 repaired as 15 entries over 47 verses, using pericopes throughout because this is a register chapter of exactly the shape the rule was written for: vv.4-7 repeat one formula word for word, vv.10-12 repeat 'abomination' three times, and the bird, insect and creeping-thing lists are catalogues. Spans: 1-2, 3, 4-8, 9-12, 13-16, 17-19, 20-23, 24-28, 29-31, 32-35, 36-38, 39-40, 41-43, 44-45, 46-47; they tile the chapter exactly. No thin exemptions — every span is richly sourced. Verse 3 kept its own entry because the two marks of the clean beast draw distinct comment from six witnesses. The old prose carried all three audit defect shapes. The chapter's real spine is a running disagreement about WHY the law exists: Clarke argues hard for a hygienic purpose and Henry, Gill and Wesley allow it a place, while Calvin refuses it three separate times in the sharpest language in the chapter ('those who imagine that God here had regard to their health... pervert by their vain speculation the whole force and utility of this law'), and Wesley finally says there was no real uncleanness in the creatures at all. That division is recorded as a debate on vv.1-2 and again on vv.44-45.

Every Jamieson, Fausset and Brown block in this chapter is foreign material: v.12 'Here are given special directions for the observance.' (a stray fragment), v.18 'All the preceding directions were communicated through the elders...' (belongs to a narrative passage, not to the cherubim), v.30 'literally, a great rabble...' (the mixed multitude of Exodus 12:38). All three omitted from the prose and declared as excluded_voices on entries 12, 18 and 30. JFB is named nowhere in the chapter.

Ellicott's block under key 40 is almost entirely StudyLight page chrome — nav menus, CSS, JS, the book_data array. The only usable sentence is his one-line cross-reference back to v.9. Gill's block under key 40 also ends in site navigation residue. Both omitted; Ellicott is therefore not named in entry 40.

Rewritten with six ranged entries (12-15, 19-20, 26-28, 32-33, 34-36, 37-38) plus one thin entry (25). The old chapter wrote all 40 verses to ~330-430 words each, which forced heavy padding on verses whose only witness is a one-line Gill gloss (v.13 45 words, v.14 39, v.28 31, v.35 95). Grouping them by what the witnesses actually treat as one unit — the ark's carrying gear, the cherubim's placement and posture, the table's rings and staves, the branches and their almond cups, the shaft and its junctions, the lamps and their tongs — gives each entry real material. Spans tile the chapter exactly.

Three entries graded B. v.21: the closing paragraph gathers the sprinkled blood (Clarke on v.17), the voice from between the cherubim (Ellicott/K&D on v.22) and the title 'ark of the testimony' into one summary — every element is in the chapter's sources, but the synthesis of them is mine. v.24: the closing paragraph infers that ark and table were built to one specification so a worshipper outside the veil could know both were of one design; the witnesses state the parallel construction but draw no such inference. vv.26-28: the closing paragraph applies the ark's 'carried, never handled' rule to the table; Ellicott states that principle only of the ark (v.15).

Four ENTITIES flags judged false positives. 'Noah' at v.10 and v.17 glosses Genesis 6:14, which Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both cite by chapter and verse (tebah as against aron; kaphar as 'to pitch'). 'Englished' at v.29 is an ordinary English verb, not a proper noun. 'Ephesus' at v.40 names the city of the silver shrines for Diana that Clarke cites from Acts 19:24 — a geographic gloss on his own citation, not a view attributed to him.

Driver/environment bug worth fixing: in the scheduled CCR container the repo is checked out with a DETACHED HEAD. synthesis-loop.py push_chapter runs 'git push -u origin master', which in that state pushes the stale local branch 'master' rather than HEAD, so every attempt is rejected as non-fast-forward and finish reports 'push rejected four times' (exit 4) even though the commit is sound and 'git push origin HEAD:master' would fast-forward. Worked around by hand this run: git checkout -B master <commit>, git reset --mixed origin/master, re-run finish --push. Suggested fix: push HEAD:master, or refuse to start when HEAD is detached.

Six Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks in this chapter carry foreign-passage material, all of it from Leviticus 25-26: v.5 on the redemption of land and the Jubilee; v.11 on the sale of houses in walled towns; v.17 on lending to a poor brother without usury; v.23 and v.29 (the same block twice) on the Hebrew servant redeemed before the Jubilee; v.47 on the barley and wheat harvests and the vintage. All six declared as excluded_voices on the covering tags entries and omitted from the prose. JFB is therefore named nowhere in the chapter.

The Ellicott block filed under v.48 ends in StudyLight page chrome — site footer, copyright text, nav menu and several kilobytes of inline CSS — which inflates the measured source for the 46-50 span by roughly 1,400 words. Not attributable to any witness, so not declarable as excluded_voices; simply omitted. The span is far too rich for the thin exemption to be in question either way.

Repaired as 13 pericope entries tiling all 50 verses: 1-2, 3, 4-7, 8-11, 12-15, 16-19, 20-22, 23-27, 28-30, 31-35, 36-40, 41-45, 46-50. The chapter's per-verse source is very unevenly distributed (v.1 alone carries 4,722 usable words, v.20 carries 15) because Henry, Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin all comment in blocks covering whole sections filed under the opening key. Splitting on the narrative seams rather than the verse boundaries keeps each entry standing on a span its own witnesses actually cover. v.3 is left alone because the rebels' speech is a self-contained unit with 799 words of comment on it. No thin exemptions: the leanest span (28-30) still carries 1,092 usable source words.

The 28-30 entry self-graded B. Henry lists the deaths that would have disproved Moses (plague, fire from heaven, the sword) and separately calls the earth opening 'a punishment without precedent'; the entry joins those into the inference that fire from heaven was named precisely because it had precedent and this appeal required something with none. The claim is sound and nothing is put into Henry's mouth, but the connective is the summary's, not his. Every other entry graded A.

Two live disagreements recorded in tags rather than smoothed over. (1) Whether Korah died in the chasm or in the fire: Ellicott and Wesley both argue for the fire, from the sons who did not die, from Deuteronomy 11:6 naming only Dathan and Abiram, and from Psalm 106:17-18 dividing the two punishments — against the plain reading of v.32 and the later summary that names Korah with the other two. (2) What metal the priests' own censers were: Gill says silver (gold only on the day of atonement) and reads the specification of brass here as marking Korah's vessels off from Aaron's; Ellicott finds no sufficient authority for silver and points to Exodus 38:3. Also recorded: Calvin holds the censers were preserved as accursed under a ban, against the commoner view that a thing once put to holy use may not return to common service.

Ellicott's note on v.40 cites the Jude parallel as 'Numbers 16:11' — a misprint for Jude 11, since the sentence is about the apostle warning Christians by this example. Written as 'the epistle of Jude' with no numeric ref rather than reproducing the bad citation.

Calvin reckons the company destroyed with Korah at 'about three hundred' where the text says two hundred and fifty; the figure is his, and the entry attributes it to him rather than correcting it silently or repeating it as fact.

Every Jamieson, Fausset and Brown block in this chapter is foreign material, drawn from Leviticus and Numbers: v.4 on the offering preceding the act of eating (Ezekiel 44:30); v.10 on the Mosaic ritual of purification and the stranger's sin of ignorance; v.16 on a man's personal sins expiated with the general body; v.22 the sabbath-breaker gathering sticks (Numbers 15); vv.34 and 40 the rebellion of Korah, Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16); v.46 the Reubenites' refusal of Moses' summons. All omitted from the prose and declared as excluded_voices on entries 3, 10, 15, 21, 34, 39 and 46. JFB is named nowhere in the chapter.

Gill's block under key 49 ends in StudyLight navigation residue ('Next: Deuteronomy Chapter 5 Sacred Texts | Bible << Previous...'). Omitted; only his gloss on the springs of Pisgah and Ashdoth-pisgah is used.

Rewritten with fourteen ranged entries and two thin ones (13, and the ranged 46-49), for 32 entries over 49 verses. The old chapter wrote all 49 to ~330-530 words apiece, which forced heavy padding on verses whose only witness is a one-line Gill gloss (v.47 has 36 source words, v.48 33, v.13 80). The spans follow the sermon's own movements — Baal-peor as evidence (3-4), the statutes taught and Israel's wisdom (5-6), the two rhetorical questions (7-8), no similitude therefore no image (15-16), the catalogue of forms (17-18), Moses excluded and the warning renewed (21-22), scattering and the gods of wood and stone (27-28), turning in tribulation and the merciful God (30-31), the purpose of the showing (35-36), the love of the fathers (37-38), know and keep (39-40), the three cities of refuge (41-43), the heading to the second address (44-45), and the closing geography (46-49). Spans tile the chapter exactly. Matthew Henry's own note says the discourse 'is so entire... that we cannot divide it into paragraphs', which is the strongest argument for grouping rather than versifying it.

Two entries graded B. v.26: the closing paragraph — that a warning delivered before the whole visible creation is harder to forget than a private one, and that Moses makes the sky over the camp and the ground under it parties to the transaction — expands Calvin's bare statement that the threat is put this way so that it may affect them more deeply. v.33: the closing paragraph generalises Calvin's contrast between individual liars and his 700,000 witnesses into a principle about why a national theophany can be appealed to as evidence; the logic is his, the statement of it as the hinge of the whole sermon is mine.

Signals judged and overridden. The 2.38x expansion on the thin entry 13 is real but harmless: the source is 80 words (Gill on why the law is called a covenant, plus Ellicott's two bare cross-references), and 190 words is the shortest honest treatment of it; Keil and Delitzsch's block under key 11 covers vv.11-13 and supplies the rest. The ENTITIES flag 'Greeks' at vv.15-16 is a false positive — Clarke writes of 'the Greek and Roman Venus' in that verse's own block.

Repaired as 12 pericope entries tiling all 57 verses: 1-3, 4-7, 8-9, 10-13, 14-18, 19-20, 21-32, 33-35, 36-38, 39-47, 48-53, 54-57. The seams are the chapter's own — the examination outside the camp, the bird rite, the two washings, the eighth-day offerings, the blood and oil, the closing sacrifices, the poor man's substitute, then the four stages of the house law, then the colophon. vv.21-32 are one entry because the section is an explicit repetition of vv.10-20 at a lower price, and vv.39-47 are one because the four verses on scraping and replastering carry only ~200 usable source words on their own — too thin for the floor, ample when read with the demolition and the quarantine rules they belong to. No thin exemptions anywhere: the leanest span (19-20) still carries 492 usable words.

Two Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks in this chapter carry foreign-passage material, both from Exodus 25 on the tabernacle furniture: v.26 holds his note on beating a winged figure out of a solid piece of gold, and v.38 his long passage on the tabernacle as a schoolmaster to Christ, the ark and mercy seat, the showbread table and the candlestick. Both declared as excluded_voices on the covering tags entries and omitted from the prose. JFB is named nowhere in the chapter.

The Ellicott block filed under v.57 ends in several kilobytes of StudyLight page chrome — inline CSS, the site's book_data array, the whole navigation menu, a Cloudflare challenge snippet and a Stripe public key — which inflates the measured source for the 54-57 span from roughly 690 real words to 1,757. Omitted silently and unnarrated. The span is comfortably above the thin threshold either way.

Three live disagreements recorded in tags rather than smoothed over. (1) Whether the seclusion was hygienic or purely ceremonial: Ellicott states flatly that leprosy was not contagious and argues it from the emptying of the house before inspection (v.36), while Wesley has the man kept out of his tent lest leprosy still lurking in him infect his family (v.8). (2) Whether house-leprosy was supernatural: Ellicott takes 'I put the plague' at face value as the immediate hand of God, Clarke answers that scripture often represents God as doing what in providence he only permits, and guesses animalcula. (3) What 'to teach' governs in v.57: Ellicott reads it as instruction against the time when the cases would have to be judged in the land, the ancient authorities and the Chaldee as instruction about which days a plague may be inspected on — Wesley's gloss, that the priest was tied to rules the people could discern as well as he could, sits with neither exactly.

The 36-38 entry self-graded B. Ellicott argues that clearing the house before the inspection shows the law did not regard leprosy as infectious; the entry adds the sharpening clause that a real infection would hardly have been let out of the door ahead of the inspection. The inference is his and the clause is faithful to it, but the formulation is the summary's. Every other entry graded A.

Repaired as 12 pericope entries tiling all 47 verses: 1-8, 9-12, 13-16, 17-19, 20-22, 23-26, 27-33, 34-36, 37-38, 39-40, 41-44, 45-47. The seams are the chapter's five controversies and their hinges — the question of authority, the parable's setting-up and its climax, the stone, the setting of the tribute trap and its answer, the Sadducees' fable and the reply to it in two parts, the scribes' commendation, the question about David's son, and the closing warning. Source is very unevenly filed: the Catena Aurea blocks for whole sections sit under the opening key (v.1, v.9, v.19, v.27, v.41, v.45), so v.9 alone carries 4,494 usable words while v.24 carries 17. No thin exemptions: the leanest span (23-26) still carries 601 usable words.

Seven Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks in this chapter are foreign-passage residue, none of them on Luke 20: v.9 and vv.33/39/45 carry stubs pointing at Matthew 10 and Matthew 18; v.15 a fragment on 'the days were being fulfilled' (Luke 9:51); v.21 his note on the disciples wanting fire from heaven on the Samaritans (Luke 9:54); v.27 a note on the second disciple's 'but' (Luke 9:59). Declared as excluded_voices on the six covering tags entries and omitted from the prose. JFB is named nowhere in the chapter.

ENTITIES flag on the 23-26 entry judged a false positive: the source header reads 'TITUS BOST;', an abbreviation the prose expands to the standard form 'Titus of Bostra'. The matcher sees 'Bostra' as an entity absent from the source; it is the same man, spelled out. Three genuine disagreements are recorded in tags instead of being smoothed over. (1) Who pronounces sentence on the husbandmen (v.16): Theophylact has the Jews give the verdict first and then recoil with 'God forbid' once they catch the parable's drift, while Augustine divides the crowd, one part answering truly and another protesting. (2) What the two fates of v.18 are: Cyril distinguishes the ruin of their souls in taking offence from the ruin of the nation in the captivity, while Bede grades them by degree and leaves the believing sinner room for penitence. (3) What the seven husbands signify (v.33): Ambrose makes the woman the synagogue, barren of spiritual offspring; Bede makes the brothers the reprobate, fruitless through the week-long course of the world.

Two kinds of misfiled but genuine material in this chapter's source, both omitted rather than used. (1) Two long Cyril of Alexandria homily blocks are filed one section late: the block under v.9 is his homily on vv.19-26 (the tribute), and the block under v.27 recapitulates the same, while the block under v.41 quotes vv.27-38 entire. Their substance is already carried by the Catena excerpts under the right verses, so nothing is lost by leaving them; using them would have credited Cyril twice for one argument. (2) Cyril of Jerusalem catechetical blocks appear under vv.37, 42 and 43 and are genuinely apposite (the Samaritans who receive only the Law; the Lord said unto my Lord; the sitting at the right hand). They were left out to avoid two different Cyrils appearing in one chapter under names a reader could not tell apart — the Catena's unqualified 'Cyril' is Cyril of Alexandria throughout.

All twelve entries self-graded A. Every claim traces to a named witness in the chapter's own source: the Catena Aurea excerpts (Augustine, Ambrose, Bede, Eusebius, Theophylact, Cyril of Alexandria, Chrysostom, Basil, Origen, Titus of Bostra) plus Gill, Henry, Calvin, Lightfoot, Ellicott, Clarke, Wesley and Robertson. No claim is put into any commentator's mouth, and no voice is named that does not comment on this chapter. Where the summary supplies a connective — 'the counter-question is not evasion', 'the parable lands, and the reaction proves it' — the assertion is one a named witness makes explicitly (Bede on the question that makes the questioners condemn themselves; Robertson's 'the cap fitted them and they saw it').

Not attempted this run (worker context exhausted; nothing is claimed, so the next --spread pick can take it freely). Survey done, recorded so the next worker need not redo it: 63 verses, 30,562 source words. It is the Judah register, and Keil and Delitzsch supply its own structure under key 21 — the towns are 'arranged in the four districts into which the land was divided': the south-land (negeb, vv.21-32), the lowland/shephelah (vv.33-47), the mountains (vv.48-60), and the desert of Judah (vv.61-62). Within those K&D further mark groups of five, six, nine and thirteen. A workable 20-entry tiling: 1; 2-4 (south border); 5-7 and 8-11 (east and north border); 12 (west); 13-14 (Caleb and the Anakim); 15-17 (Debir and Othniel); 18-19 (Achsah and the springs); 20 (heading); 21-32 (negeb); 33-36, 37-41, 42-44 (three lowland groups); 45-47 (the Philistine coast); 48-51, 52-54, 55-57, 58-60 (four mountain groups); 61-62 (wilderness); 63 (the Jebusites not driven out). The rich blocks are vv.1, 13, 14, 18, 20 and 63 (Henry 2034 words at v.13, Ellicott 1057 at v.63, Calvin 1040 at v.1); vv.21-62 are almost all one-line Gill glosses plus K&D identifications, so the register pericopes are what keep that stretch off the padding floor. Every Jamieson, Fausset and Brown block sampled here is foreign material — v.26 carries the Numbers 33 encampment list — so expect the usual chapter-wide JFB exclusion.

Repaired as 9 pericope entries tiling all 46 verses: 1-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-15, 16-18, 19-25, 26-33, 34-40, 41-46. The seams are the discourse's own — the double introduction (place, then date), the command to leave Horeb, the appointment of judges, their charge, the spies, the refusal and the appeal that failed, the oath with its exceptions, and the presumptuous attack. Source is heavily front-loaded: v.1 alone carries 4,769 usable words (Keil's and Clarke's book-level introductions plus Ellicott's geography), while v.23 carries 27. No thin exemptions: the leanest span (16-18) still carries 1,154 usable words.

Two kinds of residue in this chapter's source, both omitted silently. (1) The Clarke block under v.1 runs to roughly 2,000 words, of which a large part is publishing apparatus rather than commentary: a chapter-by-chapter table of contents for the whole book, then a catalogue of the six chronological tables Clarke appended to his own edition, with a note that the editor will have his readers' hearty thanks for the labour. Only the genuinely exegetical parts were used — the naming of the book, the five weeks it covers, and the geography of the opening verse. (2) Two Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks carry foreign-passage material: v.29 holds his note on the route of the scouts through Beth-rehob and the entering in of Hamath (Numbers 13 / 2 Samuel 10), and v.35 a note on the territory and dispersion of the Avim (Deuteronomy 2). Both declared as excluded_voices on the covering entries; JFB is named nowhere in the chapter.

Three disagreements recorded in tags rather than smoothed over. (1) Who initiated the sending of the spies (v.22): Numbers has the Lord directing it, Deuteronomy has the people asking first. Henry and Ellicott resolve it in sequence — the people proposed, Moses referred it, God permitted and so gave them up to their own counsels — while Keil and Delitzsch hold that the summons to go up is implied in the older narrative even though not stated. (2) How long they stayed at Kadesh (v.46): the repeated phrase is read either as another forty days or, as Calvin prefers, as a Hebrew idiom for an indefinite long time, from which he draws a picture of a people lying stupefied for want of knowing what to do. (3) Whether the opening verses are Mosaic (v.1): Clarke holds that the first five were added later, probably by Joshua or Ezra, which no other witness in this chapter says.

The 26-33 entry self-graded B. It opens the third paragraph by calling the charge that God hated them 'the worst sentence in the chapter, and both Ellicott and Calvin say so'. Ellicott does say it is stronger than any complaint recorded in Numbers; Calvin condemns it as malignant ingratitude and perversity but does not rank it against anything else. The judgement is sound and nothing is put into either man's mouth, but the superlative is the summary's, not theirs. Every other entry graded A.

Not attempted this run (worker context exhausted; nothing is claimed, so the next --spread pick can take it freely). Survey recorded so the next worker need not redo it. This is the largest repair unit I have been offered: 42 verses, 68,739 source words — more than twice Joshua 15 and nearly two and a half times Deuteronomy 4. Budget accordingly; a fresh worker should probably plan on this being its whole batch. Eleven witnesses, including five that do not appear in the OT chapters: John Lightfoot, Albert Barnes, A.T. Robertson, John Chrysostom and Cyril of Jerusalem. SCHOOL MAPPING IS AN OPEN QUESTION for those five and must be settled before writing, since the tags enum is fixed. A scan of all 757 stamped tag files gives only one clean signal — Albert Barnes appears as the sole voice on two verses, both tagged grammatical-historical. For the other four the corpus offers no single-voice verse, so co-occurrence counts are uninformative; read a finished NT chapter's tags directly rather than inferring. Section structure is legible from where Matthew Henry's large blocks sit (vv.1, 17, 26, plus Chrysostom at 17 and 34): Ananias and Sapphira 1-11, the signs and the growing multitude 12-16, arrest and the night release 17-26, the apostles before the council 27-32, Gamaliel's counsel and the beating 33-42. The thin verses that will need grouping are 18, 22, 23, 25, 27 and 35.

STRUCTURAL: this chapter's source is missing ten verse keys entirely — 17, 25, 31, 32, 33, 40, 41, 46, 47 and 50 — so the present keys fall into seven contiguous runs (1-16, 18-24, 26-30, 34-39, 42-45, 48-49, 51-65). A pericope range may not straddle a gap, since validate-synthesis.py expands the range and fails on 'entries cover verses absent from the source'. The first cut of this chapter used the natural tribal groupings (12-22, 23-34, 35-43, 44-51) and was rejected for exactly that reason; the spans were re-cut to sit inside the runs. Worth knowing before laying out any chapter whose source has holes: check the key set first, not just the verse count.

Repaired as 12 pericope entries tiling every present key: 1-4, 5-11, 12-16, 18-24, 26-30, 34-39, 42-45, 48-49, 51, 52-56, 57-62, 63-65. The seams follow the census itself — the command to number, Reuben with the Korah excursus, then the tribes in the order of the four camps, the total, the law of division, the Levites, and the closing verification against the Sinai roll. The tribal spans are shorter than the argument would otherwise want because of the source gaps (see the structural note), so the treatment of each tribe is split across the run boundary that falls inside it. No thin exemptions: the leanest span (48-49) carries 398 usable source words.

Nine Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks in this chapter are the same misfiled passage repeated: his note on the Kohathites being mentioned first for their connection with Aaron, on the common priests covering the sacred vessels before the Kohathites might approach, and on the exception to the rule barring entry to the holy place — all of it commentary on Numbers 4, none of it on the census. Declared as excluded_voices on every covering tags entry; JFB is named nowhere in the chapter. The Ellicott block under v.64 also ends in StudyLight page chrome (site footer, nav menu and several kilobytes of inline CSS), omitted silently.

Two disagreements recorded in tags rather than smoothed over. (1) Whether Korah died in the earthquake or the fire (v.10): Ellicott reads the Hebrew as it stands, which makes him swallowed up with Dathan and Abiram, but reports the Samaritan Pentateuch transposing the phrase so that the fire devoured Korah with the two hundred and fifty; Clarke follows the Samaritan, and Gill and Wesley reach the same result from the sense, taking the words to mean the things belonging to Korah. Note this is the same crux the loop met from the other side in Numbers 16, where the tags record it as a debate between Ellicott and Wesley on one side and the plain reading of v.32 on the other. (2) Who Jochebed was (v.59): Calvin and the plain reading make her Levi's own daughter, so that Amram married his aunt — which Calvin treats as an ingenuous confession of family dishonour that magnifies God's indulgence — while Ellicott reports the view that she was a granddaughter or remoter descendant and Amram a different man from Kohath's son.

Ten entries self-graded A; two graded B, both for the same kind of reason. The 18-24 entry closes by observing that the three southern-camp tribes all shrank while the first two of the eastern camp both grew — a juxtaposition no witness makes, though every element of it is theirs, and the prose says so explicitly rather than implying a source. The 48-49 entry ends with two cross-chapter observations of the same kind: that Naphtali, Zebulun and Dan are the only tribes whose family lists need no explanatory note, and that Naphtali's decrease alone is left without an assigned cause. Both are checkable against the chapter; neither is stated by a commentator. Also recorded: the ENTITIES flag on the Levite entry was a spelling normalisation ('Korahite' for the source's 'Korhites'), removed rather than defended.

BLOCKER — this chapter cannot be written to contract as the source stands, and the next worker will hit the same wall. Two findings. (1) The catena is incomplete: source keys are 1-32, 36, 37, 42, 48-54; verses 33-35, 38-41 and 43-47 are absent entirely. (2) An identical 207-word Jamieson, Fausset and Brown block on the tribal princes' offerings of Numbers 7 ('This tribe being stationed on the right side of Judah, offered next through its representative...') is mechanically inserted at every SIXTH key — 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54. It is unmistakable scrape residue. Keys 36 and 42 contain nothing else: QA.usable_source_words returns 0 for both after the JFB exclusion. The conflict: verse 42 is isolated (41 and 43 are not source keys), so no pericope range can absorb it without covering verses absent from the source, which coverage_problems rejects; and declaring a range ANYWHERE in the chapter switches coverage enforcement on for the whole chapter, which then demands an entry for key 42 that cannot honestly be written. Three ways out, none of which an unattended run should choose alone: (a) write the chapter with NO declared range, which leaves coverage unenforced so keys 36 and 42 can simply be omitted as residue-only, on the 2 Chronicles 27 key-16 precedent — but then several tiny verses (v.21 has 23 usable words, v.29 has 36, v.16 and v.31 have 50) must each carry a 120-word thin entry, which is padding by contract at 3-5x; (b) drop keys 36 and 42 from the source file as scrape corruption, which makes the ranged solution legal and is the cleanest fix, but edits the data tree; (c) re-scrape the chapter, since 12 of 54 verses are missing anyway. Recommend (b) or (c), owner's call. Chapter size for whoever takes it after the fix: 42 keys, 19,991 source words.

Repaired as 13 pericope entries tiling all 40 verses: 1-2, 3-5, 6-9, 10-12, 13-14, 15-19, 20-22, 23-25, 26-28, 29-33, 34, 35-36, 37-40. The seams follow Paul's own argument — the two gifts compared, the three illustrations from sound, the prayer that needs interpreting, the resolution and the five words, the quotation from Isaiah, the two visitors, the rules for tongues, the rules for prophecy, the rule about women, the appeal to the other churches, and the summing-up. v.34 stands alone because the treatment of it needs room for a genuine three-way disagreement. Source is enormous (58,535 usable words) and evenly heavy, so every entry compresses hard: expansion runs 0.06x-0.22x, the lowest ratios this loop has produced. No thin exemptions — the leanest span carries 2,529 usable words.

Three kinds of residue in this chapter's source, all omitted silently. (1) The Lightfoot block under v.1 is his note on 1 Corinthians 13:2 — 'to know all mysteries' and 'to remove mountains' — filed one chapter late. (2) Six Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks carry foreign-passage material, the one under v.5 being on Acts 24 (Tertullus and the Sanhedrim deputation); declared as excluded_voices on the six covering entries, and JFB is named nowhere in the chapter. (3) A Cyril of Jerusalem catechetical block under v.29 is on the crucifixion — the vinegar and the gall — and is not declarable as excluded_voices on that span, so it was simply omitted. The Ellicott block under v.40 also ends in StudyLight page chrome.

Four disagreements recorded in tags rather than smoothed over, and the first is the chapter's whole crux. (1) What the gift of tongues was (v.2): Ellicott argues at length that it was not languages at all — from the vocabulary (glossa never dialektos), from its never being used to preach to foreigners (the apostles did not understand Lycaonian), and from the description here of impassioned utterance expressing feeling rather than thought; Lightfoot and Clarke hold it was Hebrew, a dead language restored to the church and read there as in the synagogue. Ellicott and Calvin both note that the word 'unknown' is not in the Greek at all but was supplied by the seventeenth-century revisers, which quietly settles the question in favour of one theory wherever the AV is read. (2) What the mysteries of v.2 are: special revelations from God (Chrysostom) or dark and involved sayings of no profit (Calvin). (3) What the silence of v.34 covers: disputing and questioning on the synagogue model, leaving 1 Cor 11 and any extraordinary impulse untouched (Clarke, Wesley); public speaking generally, teaching being inconsistent with subjection, though Calvin allows a necessity may require it (Henry, Calvin); or Robertson, who declines to draw the line at all, sets Paul's plain meaning beside the daughters of Philip and the practice of his own day, and ends asking for patience rather than issuing a ruling. His refusal is recorded as a position in its own right, not flattened into one of the other two. (4) The textual variant at v.38, where Ellicott gives both readings equal weight.

Twelve entries self-graded A; one B. The 35-36 entry closes by answering Paul's two rhetorical questions in the summary's own voice — that neither can be answered in a way that leaves Corinth free to make its own rules, and that the argument has returned to the appeal to all the churches with which the section opened. Henry supplies the purpose of the questions and Ellicott the link to the churches; drawing them together into an answer is mine. Two ENTITIES flags judged false positives and left standing: 'Whitefield' where Ellicott's text spells it 'Whitfield', and 'Jerome' where Gill has 'Jerom' — both standard modern spellings of the same men, consistent with how this loop has handled Nazianzen and Tiglath-Pileser elsewhere. A third flag ('Athens', derived from Calvin's 'Athenians') was removed by rewording rather than defended.

Every Jamieson, Fausset and Brown block in this chapter is foreign material from the Pentateuch: v.17 on lawless demagogues withdrawing a city to idol-worship; v.23 the Deuteronomy 14 law against disfiguring oneself in mourning; vv.35 and 41 a bare cross-reference to Leviticus 11; v.47 the Leviticus 17 law on eating what dies of itself, with a note on the tithe. None has any bearing on the tribal registers. All omitted from the prose and declared as excluded_voices on entries 17, 22, 35, 40 and 47. JFB is named nowhere in the chapter.

Rewritten as 18 entries over 51 verses, all ranged except vv.1 and 9. The chapter is the register of the last seven lots, and it supplies its own divisions: one entry per tribal heading and then per stretch of border or town-list — 1; 2-8; 9; 10-11; 12-14; 15-16; 17-18; 19-21; 22-23; 24-26; 27-28; 29-31; 32-34; 35-39; 40-42; 43-46; 47-48; 49-51. Spans tile the chapter exactly. Every entry's source span runs 456-1571 words, so expansion is 0.38x-1.08x throughout and no thin exemption was needed anywhere — which is the point of grouping here, since per-verse entries would have had to reach 350 words from blobs as small as v.7 (17 words), v.21 (25) and v.43 (42). Worth recording for the sibling chapter: Joshua 15 has the same shape and a survey of it is already in this notebook.

Three ENTITIES flags judged false positives, all of them names the tool cannot match because of the script or inflection they carry in the source. 'Ginaea' at vv.19-21 is my transliteration of the Greek Γιναία, which Keil and Delitzsch give for the town Robinson identifies with En-gannim. 'Eleutheropolis' at vv.43-46 is their Latin accusative Eleutheropolin, in the old gazetteer's description of Gath-rimmon. The third flag, 'Gezer', was mine and is fixed: Keil and Delitzsch write Geser, quoting Josephus on Baalath, and the prose now matches them.

The sharpest disagreement in the chapter, recorded as a debate on entry 10 and worth a human's eye because it sets a prophecy against a survey. Gill, Wesley, Henry and Calvin all read Zebulun's lot as fulfilling Jacob's word that Zebulun should be a haven of ships — Calvin most strongly, calling the lot a confirmation 'as if God were twice thundering from heaven'. But Keil and Delitzsch state that the inheritance touched neither the Mediterranean nor the Jordan, and Ellicott, tracing the southern line past Jokneam, notes that it does not reach the sea because Asher's territory interposes. Both sides are given in the prose without adjudication.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown appears four times in this chapter as scrape residue only: at v.12 a block about Moses with the rod at Rephidim, at v.18 one about a bloody statute and Psalm 83:4, at v.24 one arguing an episode is out of chronological order, at v.36 one about governors hearing causes at the city gate. None touches Exodus 30. Declared as excluded_voices on entries 11, 17, 24 and 36.

Spans were re-cut twice to keep every cited voice inside its own span. Henry has no block after v.1 until v.11, so the mercy-seat lesson he draws on v.6 could not be used in the 6-x entry; Keil's atonement comment is filed under v.8, which forced 6-7 / 8-10 rather than 6-8 / 9-10. Likewise the ransom section had to split 11-12 / 13 / 14-16, since Clarke, Ellicott and Keil on the shekel all sit under v.13 while vv.14-16 carry only Gill and Ellicott; and the oil had to split 22 / 23, since Henry is at v.22 alone and Clarke, Calvin, Keil and Wesley all at v.23. Check the per-verse voice map BEFORE choosing spans, not after.
ENTITIES flagged 'Phoenicians' on both entries. Ellicott's text spells it with the oe-ligature; the prose uses the plain modern spelling. Kept, and noted in each entry's fidelity block.
Gill's block at v.38 ends with StudyLight page chrome (Next/Previous navigation and index links). Omitted silently.

Calvin's block at v.18 runs on past the laver into his entire introduction to the priesthood (Exodus 28) — several thousand words on the Levitical priest as type of Christ. Only the laver portion was used; the misfiled remainder was left alone rather than pulled into a chapter it does not belong to.

Three genuine disagreements preserved rather than smoothed: what 'his foot' was (Clarke and Ellicott a pedestal, Keil a separate drawing-vessel, Henry and Wesley a basin receiving water from spouts); what 'pure myrrh' is (Clarke has myrrh gathered by incision, Ellicott has the freely-flowing sort and calls incision-myrrh the inferior kind); and whether galbanum smelled sweet (Ellicott disagreeable but useful as a fixative, Calvin sweet, arguing from the death penalty on private use).

Not attempted (worker context exhausted; nothing claimed). 40 verses, 75,582 source words — the largest unit offered in six picks, and unlike Joshua 15 or 19 it is dense doctrinal argument on marriage and celibacy with no register structure, so pericope grouping buys almost nothing and it needs near per-verse treatment. Budget it as a whole batch for a fresh worker, or more. WORTH THE MAINTAINER'S ATTENTION, measured rather than impressionistic: --worst-first systematically hands out chapters well above corpus size. Across all 1,189 cow chapters the median is 19,611 source words and the mean 27,059; the visible head of the worst-first repair queue has a median of 30,409 and a mean of 36,482, i.e. roughly 1.55x the corpus median. The cause is structural, not a bug — defect weight counts defective verses, and verse count correlates with source size, so the worst-first ordering is also a longest-first ordering. Two consequences. (1) A batch budget should be planned around ~30k source words per chapter, not the corpus median. (2) The tail is severe: 1 Corinthians 15 sits in the current window at 116,326 words and the corpus maximum is 150,785, while 37.6% of all chapters are 25k or larger. If workers are to keep clearing the queue rather than returning surveys, the scheduled prompt's 'up to 2 chapters' is the wrong unit for this end of the queue — one chapter, or an explicit size cap on the pick, would fit it better. My own six picks bear this out: 34.7k, 28.3k, 30.6k, 68.7k, 20.0k, 18.9k and now 75.6k.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown appears five times in this chapter as scrape residue, every block belonging to Exodus 30-31: the laver at v.1, the anointing oil at v.7, the oil again at v.13, the incense at v.19, and Bezaleel's skill at v.31. None touches Leviticus 7. Declared as excluded_voices on entries 1, 5, 12, 19 and 28.

Ellicott's block at v.37 runs off into StudyLight page chrome — stylesheet rules, the whole nav menu, a Cloudflare challenge snippet, a Stripe public key and the full book_data array. Gill's block at v.38 ends with Next/Previous index links. Omitted; only the commentary proper was used.

Per-verse voice map was built BEFORE spans were chosen this time, and it drove the boundaries. Henry has blocks only at vv.1, 11, 28 and 35, and the v.1 block is his overview of the whole first section, so his material on the skin and the meat offerings had to sit inside the 1-4 entry rather than the 8-10 one. Calvin appears only at 6, 11, 16, 19, 23 and 37. Spans were laid out so every cited voice falls inside its own span, and the used-vs-present check returned zero ghosts on the first pass.

Four genuine disagreements preserved: how wide the occasion for a thanksgiving offering runs (Jarchi, Aben Ezra and Ellicott confine it to notable deliverances, Gill extends it to the common mercies of life); what marks off the second class of peace offering (Ellicott's canon-law distinction between a vow binding the person and a freewill offering binding only the animal, against Calvin's reading that the vow meant here is simple rather than conditional, since a conditional vow paid would be thanksgiving); where the laws were given (Gill reads 'in mount Sinai' as by or near it, after the tabernacle stood, while Clarke has them given on the mount itself); and what 'the law of the consecrations' names (Ellicott the high priest's meat offering on entering office, Wesley the sacrifice at the consecration of the priests).

Clarke's block at v.8 carries a long Virgil quotation on sleeping upon sacrificial fleeces for dreams and an equally long note from Sir Walter Scott on the Highland togharm. Both are Clarke's own comparative material, so they were summarised rather than quoted, and kept — they are the most distinctive thing in the chapter's catena.

Entries 1 and 28 first graded B on repetition — low type-token ratio, not duplicated content (dupfrac 0.000 on both). The cause is the chapter's own vocabulary: offering, trespass, sin, peace, burnt, altar, priest, breast, shoulder recur unavoidably. Fixed by deliberately varying the surrounding prose rather than by cutting substance, which took both to A. Worth expecting on any Leviticus sacrifice chapter.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown is scrape residue throughout this chapter — twelve verses carry a JFB block and not one of them is about Joshua 15. The recurring texts are from Deuteronomy 9-10 (the golden calf, the tables of stone) and Deuteronomy 4-6 (the repetition of precepts). Declared as excluded_voices on eleven of the sixteen entries.

Ellicott's blocks at v.37 and v.63 both run off into StudyLight page chrome: stylesheet rules, the full nav menu, a Cloudflare challenge snippet, a Stripe public key and the book_data array. Omitted; only the commentary proper was used.

A 63-verse boundary-and-town-list chapter, 30,562 source words, cut into sixteen entries. The voice map drove every span: Henry has blocks only at vv.1, 13, 20 and 28-35, Calvin only at 1, 13, 14, 18, 20 and 63, and both write section overviews rather than verse notes, so their material had to be used inside the entry covering the verse it is filed under. Two ghost attributions surfaced in the first check — Henry's Bethlehem remark and his note on the wilderness being thinly settled, both from the v.20 block, quoted in the 55-60 and 61-62 entries — and were rewritten out. The town lists (21-62) are mostly Gill and Keil at 200-300 words a verse; grouping them by the chapter's own district headings gives entries of workable length at expansion ratios of 0.15x to 0.36x.

Seven disagreements preserved rather than smoothed: whether the lot governed the division among families as well as tribes (Gill against Clarke and Wesley); what the river of Egypt is (Clarke calls it undecidable, Ellicott and Keil name the Wady el-Arish); where the valley of Hinnom lay (Jerome and Clarke east of Jerusalem, Reland and Keil south of Zion); when Caleb drove out the Anakim (Gill before Joshua's death, Calvin after); how Othniel was related to Caleb (Gill makes him a nephew to save the marriage from the incest law, Keil makes him Caleb's own younger brother and denies the law applies); why the town totals do not match the names (Simeon's transfer, the definition of a city, or corrupt compound names); why Gath and Ashkelon are unnamed (Gill's 'the three stand for the rest' against Keil's 'both lie inside the boundaries already given'); and how habitable the desert of Judah was (Keil's terrible desert against Gill's many cities and villages).

Clarke at v.58 reports that the Alexandrian and Vatican manuscripts of the Septuagint insert eleven further towns here, Ephratha (Bethlehem) among them, that Jerome knew them, and that Kennicott would restore them, explaining the loss as a transcriber's eye skipping between two occurrences of 'and their villages'. Keil independently records the same gap. This bears directly on Henry's remark at v.20 that Bethlehem's absence shows how little the town then was — if the eleven belong, the absence is a copyist's slip. The two are filed under different verses and so sit in different entries; the connection is drawn in the 55-60 entry without attributing Henry's remark there.

Two ENTITIES flags kept deliberately. 'Hadireh' is the source's 'Hadîreh' with the circumflex stripped. 'Onomasticon' expands the source's standing abbreviation 'Onom.' — same class as the Whitfield/Jerom spellings kept in earlier chapters. Four other flags were genuine and were fixed: 'Anakim' (Calvin spells it Enakim, Keil Anakites) reworded away; 'Masoretes' (source has Masorites) reworded to the received accentuation; 'Watchtower' was my translation of Keil's Alba Specula and was reverted to the Latin; 'Safieh' and 'Esdud' were misspellings of the source's Saphieh and of a mangled Esdûd.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown appears three times as scrape residue, none of it on Deuteronomy 2: at v.6 a fragment about rescuing ambassadors (2 Kings 6), at v.24 a passage about nomad tribes at the base of the Idumean mountain, at v.30 one about the scouts who did not join the mutinous murmuring. Declared as excluded_voices on entries 4, 24 and 26.
Ellicott's block at v.36 runs off into StudyLight page chrome — stylesheet rules, the nav menu and the site footer. Omitted; only the commentary proper was used.

Ten entries over 37 verses, 14,593 source words. Henry writes only three blocks in this chapter (vv.1, 8 and 24) and each is a section overview covering many verses ahead, so his material had to be used inside the entry containing the verse it is filed under: his treatment of the ban on the Amorites sits under v.24 and therefore in the 24-25 entry, not in 33-35 where the slaughter is actually narrated. The first ghost check caught exactly that, plus Calvin quoted in 20-23 from his v.19 block and Clarke quoted in 17-19 from his v.20 block; all three were rewritten out. Worth noting that the ghost check does NOT catch the subtler error — attributing out-of-span material to a voice who happens to have some other block inside the span — which is how Ellicott's v.21 argument nearly stayed in the 17-19 entry.

Four disagreements preserved: how God could be said to have blessed the work of Israel's hands in a desert with no commerce (Calvin says their cattle increased and their labour yielded furniture and necessaries though they earned no wages; Ellicott sees nothing unreasonable in supposing ordinary trade, since they had skilled workmen); whether the Emim and Rephaim were giants (Gill and Wesley take the stature literally, Clarke insists Rephaim is a people's name and that fear and public report added the height); whether the embassy to Sihon preceded the command to attack (Calvin rearranges the verses into a pluperfect parenthesis, Keil and Henry keep the order and read the peace offer as leaving Sihon inexcusable); and what the hardening of Sihon's spirit means (Wesley's permissive 'suffered it to be hardened', Keil's judgment of hardening, and Ellicott's argument that God gave the strength and the same verb tells Joshua to be of good courage).

One ENTITIES flag fixed and two kept. 'Troglodytes' was corrected to the source's 'Troglodytae'. 'Jerome' is Gill's 'Jerom' in modern spelling, and 'Wady Mojib' is Ellicott's 'Wady Mojib' with the circumflexes stripped — both the same class of orthographic variant kept and noted in Exodus 30 and Joshua 15.

The three commentators who speak to the extermination of Sihon's people (Ellicott, Wesley, Keil) all press the same way: Ellicott insists the word will bear nothing less than devotion to destruction and that the narrative therefore asserts an extermination by express divine command, Wesley grounds it in the wickedness of the devoted nation, Keil describes the ban without qualification. None offers the softening reading. Henry alone, under v.24, enters the limiting principle — that the case was extraordinary and is not a precedent for war without quarter — which is recorded there rather than at 33-35 because that is where his block sits.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown appears three times as scrape residue, none of it on Exodus 26: at v.13 and v.31 fragments about the Shekinah cloud and the angel of God, at v.37 more of the same. Declared as excluded_voices on entries 7, 31 and 36.

Ellicott's block at v.37 runs off into StudyLight page chrome — stylesheet rules, the full nav menu, a Cloudflare challenge snippet, a Stripe public key and the book_data array. Omitted; only the commentary proper was used.

Eight entries over 37 verses, 16,361 source words. The spans were re-cut once mid-draft: an entry keyed 22-25 had absorbed the bars (vv.26-29), whose commentary is filed under v.26 and later. The ghost check did NOT catch this, because Ellicott, Gill and Keil all have blocks inside 22-25 as well — the same blind spot recorded for Deuteronomy 2. Fixed by merging 22-25 and 26-30 into a single 22-30 entry, which also brought a thin pair up to a workable length. The lesson stands: the ghost check verifies that a cited voice is somewhere in the span, not that the material cited is.

Three disagreements preserved. On the thickness of the boards, Keil and Delitzsch reject both Josephus' four fingers and the cubit proposed by Rashi and Bahr, on the ground that a cubit-thick board could neither be cut from an acacia nor carried on a desert road. On the proportion of the two chambers, Keil gives ten cubits and twenty while Ellicott points out that 'under the taches', read strictly, makes them equal, and floats the Temple's half-size arrangement as a third possibility. On the word describing the door hanging, Ellicott builds his whole inwoven-versus-embroidered distinction on it, while Keil denies it means embroidery at all and holds for stripes or checks woven in mixed colours.

Two things in this chapter's catena are worth flagging for anyone working the tabernacle chapters. Calvin opens at v.1 by refusing the allegorical method outright — it was by no means God's intention to include mysteries in every hook and loop, and even if no part were without mystical meaning, which no one in his senses will admit, it is better to confess ignorance than indulge conjecture. He names the writer to the Hebrews as his model of restraint. And at v.36 Keil and Delitzsch publicly retract a reading they had printed in their own earlier Archaeologie, naming the Rabbins, Gesenius and Bahr as fellow-mistaken; the retraction unsettles Ellicott's distinction at v.1, so the two are recorded as a debate rather than harmonised.

Zero ENTITIES signals on the whole chapter — the first clean fidelity read-back in this run. The reason is probably that Exodus 26 has almost no place-names and no modern site identifications; the flags in Exodus 30, Joshua 15 and Deuteronomy 2 were nearly all transliterated toponyms or diacritics stripped from surveyors' spellings.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown is scrape residue at six verses in this chapter, none of it on Exodus 29: fragments about the wilderness murmuring, the quails and the tamarisk manna, and the faithful scouts. Declared as excluded_voices on entries 4, 15, 22, 26, 35 and 38.
Ellicott's block at v.46 runs off into StudyLight page chrome (footer, terms-of-use links). Omitted; only the commentary proper was used.

Eleven entries over 46 verses, 20,291 source words. One ghost attribution caught before validating: Keil and Delitzsch quoted in the 43-46 entry, where their block actually sits at v.42 and so falls in the 38-42 span. Replaced with Clarke and Ellicott, who do have blocks at 43-46. Six other entries first showed a substantive voice as excludable — Gill at v.1, Gill in 4-9, Wesley and Clarke in 15-18, Ellicott and Wesley in 26-34, Clarke in 38-42, Gill in 43-46 — in every case because I had simply not used a commentator who had real material there. All six were written in rather than declared excluded; excluded_voices is for residue, not for a writer's omissions.

One three-way disagreement preserved, on 'whatsoever toucheth the altar shall be holy'. Calvin reads it of the offerings, the altar sanctifying the victims laid on it, and notes but rejects the masculine reading that would make it the priest. Clarke reads it as property: whatever was laid on the altar became the Lord's and had to be wholly devoted. Ellicott turns the grammar round and makes it a prohibition — 'must be holy', nothing unholy may touch it, the future carrying imperative force as in the Ten Commandments.

Three passages in this catena are unusually rich and worth knowing about. Clarke at v.22 relays Houbigant's conjecture that the waving and heaving of the offerings traced the figure of the cross, and is careful to present it as a conjecture he will not assert. Clarke at v.30 turns the seven days into a full excursus on the number seven — the Hebrew number of perfection, the Essene formula preserved by Philo and Josephus, the Pythagorean triangle and square, Cicero's 'knot and cement of all things' — and ends by leaving the ancient philosophers to judge their own meaning. Calvin at v.38 refuses to let the oil and wine of the daily offering be read as flavouring, since God was not gratified by their savour and did not wish to make epicures of the priests under colour of religion.

Zero ENTITIES signals again, as in Exodus 26 — these tabernacle and consecration chapters carry almost no place-names. But two entries first graded B on repetition (2-3 and 19-21, ttr 0.562 and 0.579, dupfrac 0.000). The cause is the same as in Leviticus 7: the chapter's own vocabulary — bread, cake, unleavened, oil, blood, hands — recurs unavoidably. Fixed by varying the surrounding prose rather than cutting substance, which took both to A.

The numbering section (34-49) had to be split at 44 because the whole of it as one entry ran 890 words. The split is uneven on purpose: Henry, Calvin, Keil and Clarke all have their blocks filed at vv.34-36, so everything substantive lives in 34-43, and 44-49 carries only Wesley at v44, Ellicott at v48 and Gill's closing note at v49 — 414 words, the tightest entry in the chapter but clear of the floor.

Gill is declared in excluded_voices for the 34-43 entry. He is present in every verse of that span but only as lemma stubs and 'See Gill on' cross-references — there is no exposition to synthesise. This is residue in the scrape, not an omission of mine; the ghost check reported him as declarable because his name recurs so often.

JFB is residue throughout this chapter: every JFB block is Leviticus 14 leper-purification material (the two birds, the trespass offering, the log of oil), unrelated to Numbers 4. Declared in excluded_voices on every entry whose span contains one. Verse 48 additionally carries StudyLight page chrome — the CSS block, the nav menu and the commentary index — which is why 'Adam Clarke' appears in the 44-49 blob without Clarke having any note there.

Two ENTITIES signals came from my own glosses, not the sources, and both were removed. At vv.9-14 I had expanded Ellicott's bare cross-reference to Numbers 13:23 into 'the cluster of Eshcol'; at vv.17-20 I had expanded Keil's bare citation of 1 Samuel 6:19 into 'the men of Beth-shemesh'. Both facts are true and neither is in the catena — filling in a proper name a commentator only pointed at is an attribution the source does not carry.

Clarke's table as scraped is internally corrupt: it prints 22,300 Levites in all with '3,580 fit for service and 13,720 unfit', where 8,580 + 13,720 = 22,300. I reported the two figures that add (22,300 total, 13,720 unfit) and left the garbled one alone. The live disagreement is real and worth keeping: Clarke's addition of the two censuses gives 22,300, while Keil and Ellicott both put the tribe at 22,000.

Ellicott and Wesley read the Gershonite load in opposite orders. Ellicott makes the first item the fine twined linen curtains of the mishkan (holding the woodwork subsidiary to them) and the goats' hair the tent's; Wesley makes the first item the goats' hair covering and the second the ten linen curtains. Kept as a debate rather than smoothed — the two readings assign the same objects to different phrases.

The catena for this chapter has no keys 10, 11 or 39, so pericope spans cannot be drawn freely: coverage_problems fails any entry covering a verse absent from the source. Spans therefore break at 9|12 (entry '3' runs 3-9, the next starts at 12) and the chapter's last entry stops at 38 rather than 39. Tiling verified at 36 keys.

JFB is residue everywhere in this chapter. Every JFB block is Exodus 26-27 material — the boards that formed the walls, the five cross bars and the middle bar, the dimensions of the brazen altar and its horns, the court's sixty brazen pillars — filed under Exodus 40 verses. Declared in excluded_voices on every entry whose span contains one.

Keil and Delitzsch appear at v2 and again at v35 as bare scripture text with no comment attached: the block quotes Exodus 40:2-9 and 40:35-38 verbatim and stops. Declared in excluded_voices on both entries rather than cited. Keil's substantive notes in this chapter sit at vv.18, 21, 23 and 30, and are used there.

The span ghost check caught a real misattribution. My first draft of the v2 entry credited Henry, alongside Wesley, with the computation that the first day of the first month fell fourteen days short of a year from the exodus. Henry's block is filed at v1, not v2; only Wesley carries that material within the span. Rewritten to Wesley alone, whose v2 note also supplies the Hezekiah precedent and the observation about the new moon — both of which the first draft had dropped.

Entries '1' and '27' first graded B on lexical variety (ttr 0.548 and 0.545) with dupfrac 0.000, no repeated n-grams and no duplicate sentences — nothing a reader would call repetition. The cause was density of function words in long 'the X of the Y' chains plus the chapter's own unavoidable nouns (tabernacle, altar, door, place, hanging). Both were rewritten with more varied diction and shorter genitive chains rather than cut for length, taking ttr to 0.705 and 0.692 and the chapter to 100 percent grade A.

Three readings of the tent spread abroad over the tabernacle, kept as a debate rather than smoothed. Gill takes it for the goats'-hair curtains; Clarke for the whole set of coverings of rams' skins and goats' hair thrown over the building, the tabernacle having no other roof; Ellicott separates the verse's two clauses, making the goats' hair the ohel proper and the rams' and seals' skins the miksêh laid above it.

Calvin denies the premise the chronological notes rest on. He cannot approve the opinion that the tabernacle was only now set up: it was complete before Moses' second ascent, and had stood pitched outside the camp in token of divorce since the golden calf, so the setting-up means its restoration to its proper place in the midst of the people. Clarke and Ellicott both reckon the dates on the opposite assumption. Recorded as a debate on the '2' entry.

JFB is residue in this chapter as elsewhere, and Keil's blocks at vv.2, 14 and 23 are bare scripture quotation with no comment attached — the text of the following verses reprinted and nothing more. Both declared in excluded_voices rather than cited. Keil is also excluded at the 30-32 entry, but for a different reason worth distinguishing: his block there quotes vv.30-33 and then comments on v.33, which falls outside that entry's span, so nothing in it is usable where it sits.

Two scrape defects in this chapter. Calvin's block at v.14 ends with an enormous scripture-index dump — several hundred bare references running from Genesis through the Psalms — appended after his comment on the four standards; it is StudyLight page furniture, not text. Gill's block at v.29 is a bare lemma, 'And Moses said unto Hobab, the son of Raguel the Midianite,' with no exposition following, so Gill is declared excluded on the Hobab entry.

Clarke came up excludable at two entries on the first ghost pass, and in both cases the fault was mine rather than the source's. His v.2 note (why two instruments could reach so vast an army, the pair differing in length and pitch, Josephus reserving one for the nobles) and his v.14 note (the whole marching order as a bare table) are real content that I had simply not used. Both were written in rather than excluded — excluded_voices is for residue, not for a writer's omissions.

The sound of the teruah is disputed three ways and cannot be harmonised. Gill hears a broken, uneven, quavering note and reaches for the onomatopoeia tara-tan-tara; Clarke agrees on the roughness and derives it from the Roman taratantara; Ellicott holds the exact opposite, that teruah is a loud unbroken blast distinguished from the convocation signal precisely by its continuity; Keil and Delitzsch relocate the contrast into the verbs, making one short sharp bursts and the other a sustained peal. Kept as a debate.

Calvin and Gill contradict each other outright on the three days' journey. Calvin reads a continuous three-day march, arguing that no tents were pitched until Paran and the people slept in the open air; Gill separates the stages, placing a month at Taberah and seven days at Hazeroth between them, and sets Bunting's eight miles from Sinai against the Targum of Jonathan's thirty-six. Both recorded; the entry does not adjudicate.

Calvin reverses the usual sense of 'thou mayest be to us instead of eyes' and says so explicitly, complaining that commentators do not appear to have observed the construction. Where Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott read the clause prospectively — Hobab is wanted for desert knowledge the cloud does not supply — Calvin insists the Hebrew carries more than one causal particle, making it retrospective: Hobab has already served as eyes and borne the inconveniences, and would forfeit his recompense by leaving now.

Drafting for lexical variety from the outset — short genitive chains, concrete nouns, varied verbs — held every entry in this chapter at grade A with no repetition-repair pass, where Exodus 40 needed two entries rewritten after they graded B on ttr alone. The remaining cost is still the ceiling: most first drafts landed 40 to 170 words over 650. The 21-28 entry ran the other way and had to be grown from 300 to 390, since that span is almost entirely 'See Gill on' stubs with only Gill at vv.21, 25 and 28, Wesley at v.21 and Ellicott at v.28 carrying content.

Numbers 33 has no keys 26 or 27, so spans had to break at 25|28. It is also one of the chapters the quality audit names as known-degenerate (ttr 0.31-0.37 alongside Joshua 17), and the reason is visible in the source: vv.19-36 are mostly one-line Clarke entries saying a place is unknown, with Gill supplying mileages and nothing else. Wide spans (16-25, 28-40, 41-49) were the only way to reach the floor without padding, and the middle entries are built almost entirely from Clarke's site identifications and Gill's distances.

JFB is residue throughout as usual. Two further exclusions are of a different kind: Keil's blocks at v.17 and v.55 are bare scripture quotation with no comment (declared excluded on the 16-25 and 55-56 entries), and Ellicott at v.40 is a single cross-reference, 'See Numbers 21:1, and Note' (excluded on 28-40). Verse 56 additionally carries the StudyLight CSS and nav-menu chrome after Ellicott's note, and Calvin's block at v.14 of the neighbouring chapter has the same defect.

Three ENTITIES signals, all of them my own tidying of the source rather than anything the sources said. I had written Elanitic where the scrape has Elantic, Moserah where Gill has Mosera, and Idumean where Clarke has 'a place in Idumea'. All three reverted to the source forms — including the apparent typo Elantic, on the Deuteronomy 2 precedent of keeping a source's orthography rather than silently correcting it. The general lesson is the same one the Numbers 10 note recorded: adjectives and normalised spellings I supply are attributions the catena does not carry.

A third word-count in the pipeline, worth knowing about. Entry 41-49 measured 647 by synthesis_qa.visible (which is what validate-synthesis uses and what the finish validator gates on) but 651 by audit-synthesis-quality's own tokeniser, which put it in the 651+ length bucket. My regex spot-check gave 639. Three counters, three answers; drafting to about 640 by QA.visible keeps clear of all of them.

Why Taberah is missing from the itinerary. Gill gives two answers — either it was the same place as Kibroth-hattaavah or lay beside it, or, on Aben Ezra's view, Israel camped there only one day and so it does not rank among the journeys. Clarke reasons from distance instead: three days' march were needed to reach this point, so other stations must have stood between and gone unrecorded because they were unremarkable. The two explanations are not compatible, since Clarke's makes the list selective and Gill's makes it complete.

Where Aaron died. Deuteronomy has Israel reaching Mosera from Bene-jaakan and places Aaron's death there; this chapter reverses the order and puts the death at Hor. Gill follows Jarchi in supposing they doubled back (Hashmonah to Mosera, then Bene-jaakan, then Mosera again, the two places twenty-four miles apart); Clarke resolves it geographically, making Mosera, Moseroth and Hor three names for one site, or Moseroth a village near the mountain. Recorded as a debate rather than harmonised.

Whether the gods of Egypt were literally overthrown. Wesley takes the clause doubly — the false gods were the beasts the Egyptians worshipped, which died when the firstborn of man and beast were struck, and their images too were probably thrown down as Dagon was before the ark. Calvin calls it a silly imagination that every idol toppled of itself, holding that God triumphed over them by proving they could not help their worshippers and by exposing the magicians' trickery.

JFB is residue throughout, as usual. Keil's block at v.34 is bare scripture quotation with no comment attached (his substantive notes in this stretch sit at vv.32-33 and were used on the 31-33 entry), so he is declared excluded on 34-36. Verse 34 also carries the full StudyLight page chrome after Ellicott's note — CSS, nav menu, the commentary index and the Cloudflare and Stripe snippets.

The 18-21 span has only 481 source words and my first draft came in at 313, under the floor. Rather than pad it I re-expanded from the same material to 414 by giving each commentator's note its full statement instead of a compressed one — a 0.86x ratio, high but honest, and the same remedy that worked on Exodus 40's 18-19 entry. Verse 25 was folded into the 22-25 span so that Ellicott's correction of the rump to the fat-tail had somewhere to live rather than being stranded in a one-verse entry.

Three of the long blocks in this chapter are section overviews filed well before the verses they discuss. Henry at v.1 covers the washing, vesting and anointing of vv.6-13; Calvin at v.10 covers the imposition of hands and the blood on ear, thumb and toe at vv.22-24; Henry at v.31 covers everything through v.36. Under the filing rule that material has to be used in the entry containing the verse it is filed under, so the 6-9 and 22-25 entries are built from Ellicott, Gill, Keil and Clarke while Henry's and Calvin's treatments of the same acts appear earlier.

What figure was drawn on the high priest's forehead after the oil was poured. Gill reports Jarchi and Maimonides, who have the anointer draw the oil between the eyebrows in the shape of a Greek chi; Ellicott reports the practice of the second Temple, which made the figure a Caph, the initial letter of the word for priest. Both are traditions rather than exegesis, and neither commentator acknowledges the other's.

Whether the anointing oil and the blood were mixed before sprinkling. Gill takes the wording, which runs the two together, to mean they were combined; Ellicott holds that it cannot possibly be gathered either from this verse or from the Exodus passage prescribing the rite whether they were sprinkled separately or mingled first. Recorded as a debate: Gill infers where Ellicott declines to.

Who killed the ram of the burnt offering. Gill says Moses, citing the Septuagint, and Ellicott agrees that although the offerer ordinarily slaughtered his own victim, Moses acted here as he had at the sin offering. Wesley leaves room for a deputy — the verb may mean Moses or some other person acting by his appointment — and finds a reason for the vagueness in the text naming Moses expressly for the sprinkling of the blood, an act more properly priestly and more essential to the sacrifice.

Clarke's comparison of the consecration with the Roman taurobolium is the most striking single note in the chapter, and its direction is worth preserving exactly. He does not treat the Hebrew rite as a variant of the pagan one: he judges the Roman ceremony to bear a striking allusion to Aaron's consecration, to have probably been borrowed from it, and then to have been disguised by Rome's own superstitions. He returns to it at v.36 to make the chapter's whole logic turn on it — these rites are significant taken in reference to Christ's priesthood, and taken out of that relation would be as absurd and nugatory as the making of a Roman pontiff.

Five JFB blocks in this chapter are scrape residue from Acts 13-14, not comment on Romans 11: v2 carries a fragment on Elymas and the proconsul, v8 a 220-word travel narrative on Perga and Pisidian Antioch (Howson quoted), v14 'cherished he them (as a nurse the infant in her bosom)', v20 a note on David's seed and the name Jesus, v26 a fragment on Gentile proselytes and 'the Jew first'. JFB has no genuine comment anywhere in Romans 11. None were declared as excluded_voices because no verse needed the thin exemption; they were simply ignored, as the prose rules require.

Three further residue blocks: Lightfoot at v10 is a Prov 27:22 note plus running page headers ('HOR HEBRAICHZ ET TALMUDICE'); Lightfoot at v22 opens with a Rom 8:22 fragment before turning to a genuine preface on Romans 11 (the on-topic half was used); Ellicott at v36 is ~100 words of real comment followed by ~1,150 words of StudyLight page furniture — nav menus, CSS and inline JavaScript. Names quoted INSIDE a block are not voices. Calvin's editorial apparatus here names Chrysostom, Origen, Ambrose, Augustine, Grotius, Pareus, Beza, Griesbach, Mede and Turrettin; the UNSOURCED check is chapter-level, so it passes on any of them who comment elsewhere in the chapter and will not catch the error. Voices were therefore derived by intersecting the names used in the prose with the names that actually head a block in that verse's own catena. That caught three real misattributions before they landed (Calvin at v4, Henry at v5 and v36) and three near-misses (Chrysostom at 15, 32, 33, where Calvin's editor is merely quoting him).

Three axes run the length of this chapter and are worth carrying into Romans 9-10 and Galatians. (1) 'Life from the dead' at v15: Calvin argues from the sentence's balance that it must describe a revival among the Gentiles, and names Chrysostom and Theodoret as holding the last-resurrection reading he rejects; Theodoret's own block confirms it exactly, and Ellicott sides with him. (2) 'All Israel' at v26: Gill insists on the Jewish nation as a body and names the corporate reading as the one he rejects; Calvin takes it for the whole people of God from both, appealing to Galatians 6:16; Theodoret at v27 independently agrees with Calvin; Robertson sets both out and declines. (3) 'Without repentance' at v29: Barnes makes it secure perseverance, while Theodoret argues from Saul, Solomon and the Jews themselves that God does resume gifts on ingratitude, and points to the Gentile threat at v22. In each case the Antiochene voice is on the opposite side from the one a reader would predict from the chapter's Reformed centre of gravity.

REFINEMENT to the sizing model this worker has been building across batches 15-22: key count predicts cost only AFTER honest grouping, and how much grouping is honest depends on chapter genre. Three regimes. (a) Narrative and argument — romans 11, genesis 31, genesis 37, judges 9 and 11: the witnesses say something distinct about nearly every verse, so entries roughly equal keys and key count is the true cost. (b) Liturgical or legal repetition — leviticus 26, with its four matched seven-times-more cycles: real grouping available, maybe 46 keys down to 12. (c) Register or diagnostic manuals — leviticus 13 is the extreme case, and the loop doc's own example (Numbers 7's twelve identical tribal offerings) is the same shape. Leviticus 13 is a clinical loop: the priest shall look, shut up seven days, look again on the seventh day, pronounce clean or unclean, repeated through bright spot, scall, boil, burning, baldness and garment. Sampled keys 29-32 run 365, 624, 314 and 114 words and say the same procedural thing each time; the median of 278 across 59 keys is itself the signature. Written per-verse this produces dozens of near-identical write-ups, which is precisely the templating defect the audit exists to catch — so per-verse here is not merely expensive, it is WRONG. Under honest tiling by case-type it is probably 10-14 entries, cheaper than anything else in the queue. Practical upshot for the picker: a low median-words-per-key alongside a high key count is the fingerprint of regime (c), and is a signal that the chapter is cheap and should be tiled, not that it is thin and expensive.

Two clusters of named disagreement worth carrying into Numbers 4 and 26. (1) The arithmetic at 38-39: the three houses total 22,300 while the muster is recorded as 22,000, and the recorded figure must stand because the whole redemption depends on the firstborn exceeding the Levites by exactly 273. Henry (at his key 14 block) gives the traditional reconciliation, that the 300 were firstborn Levites already sanctified and so unable to enter the exchange; Keil and Delitzsch weigh that and reject it as forced and unsatisfactory, since an account this circumstantial would not have omitted the fact, and posit a copyist's error in the Kohathite figure; Clarke independently posits the same class of error in the Gershonite figure, two Hebrew letters for 200 and 500 being easily confounded. Three named solutions, two of them textual. (2) How the 273 were picked at 40-51: Gill reports the rabbinic lot from Jarchi, Abarbinel and the Talmud without endorsing it; Clarke calls that a most stupid and silly tale and prefers a general fund; Henry and Wesley suppose the exchange ran from the eldest downward so the youngest 273 paid; Ellicott says the text simply does not record it and offers the most-recently-born or the lot.

Ellicott at 44-51 denies outright what this chapter is usually taken to prove — that a priesthood of the firstborn was transferred to the Levites — calling the assertion altogether without foundation on three grounds: the patriarchal priesthood was not restricted to the firstborn but belonged to the head of every family; it was exercised before the exodus and so before the command to sanctify the firstborn existed; and it was thenceforth confined to Aaron's family, who inherited it not as substitutes for the firstborn but in the place of the whole nation. Every other witness in the chapter writes as though the transfer is the point of the arrangement, so this is a genuine outlier rather than a nuance. Worth checking against Numbers 8 and 18, where the same substitution is restated.
