The reason is that most of the chapter is a gazetteer: vv.16-20 and 25-27 are strings of place-names with one- and two-line notes from Gill, Clarke and Wesley, which distil at a much higher ratio than argued exposition. Confirms the sizing corollary from note 384 in the other direction: density of distinct ARGUMENTS per source word, not source words alone, sets the entry count. Where a span is mostly toponymy, a long span is safe; where it is mostly argument (genesis 11:6-9), a short one is not.

JFB scrape residue, twenty-sixth chapter affected. All six JFB blocks are Leviticus 8-9 material (the consecration of Aaron), in narrative order, keyed at 3, 9, 15, 27, 33, 45. This confirms all three predictions of the period-6 model formed at numbers 21 and exodus 23: the keys are arithmetic (period 6, offset 3 here — the offset varies between chapters, the period does not), the donor chapter is walked in order, and the scraper stalls and repeats (keys 9 and 15 are byte-identical, md5 8328d0b4). New refinement: the sequence has EMPTY SLOTS — 21 and 39 carry no JFB block at all — so a mechanical sweep must look for period-6 sequences that skip positions, not just unbroken runs. Excluded from all entries covering these keys.

Scrape overrun at the LAST key of the chapter, fourth confirmation of this defect after joshua 24, numbers 11 and leviticus 22. Key 46 is 34,286 characters, of which the tail carries minified JavaScript (event binding for the study-desk ref links and a navigation accordion). New variant: the junk is NOT at the end of the block stream but sits MID-STREAM, between the Ellicott block and the Wesley block, so a fix that only truncates the tail of the last key will not catch this shape. The invariant remains position — always the chapter's final key — not content type. usable_source_words overstates key 46 accordingly.

Block-keying loss declared for entries 18-26 and 27-39. Matthew Henry's exposition of the entire curse section (verses 14-39, including the escalating chastisements, the desolation, the scattering and the sabbaths of the land) is keyed at verse 14 as one block; there is no Henry block anywhere at 18 or 27. His material was used in entry 14-17, where it is keyed, and the two later entries therefore carry no puritan-evangelical voice. The loss is recorded in each entry's outliers rather than distorted into the tiling. The Henry block at 14 also concatenates his Complete exposition with his Concise commentary on the chapter.

Wesley abridges Henry, third book of confirmation after exodus 23 and genesis 21. Two clean instances here. At 16 Henry writes that all chronical diseases are included in the consumption and all acute in the burning ague or fever; Wesley's whole note on the clause is that sentence. At 46 Henry ends on the law as the bond of communion — God manifesting not only his dominion but his favour by giving them his law, they manifesting not only holy fear but holy love by observing it, so that it is made between them rather as a covenant than a law, for he draws with the cords of a man — and Wesley's note is the same sentences with trivial variation. Consequence for the tally, as logged before: Wesley agreeing with Henry is one witness, not two, and counting puritan-evangelical and wesleyan-arminian separately overstates agreement.

Ten women baking at one oven (v26). The usual view, held by Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott and Bush, is scarcity: one oven suffices for ten families where ordinarily it served one, and the bread is returned by stinted weight. Calvin argues the reverse — that Moses means there shall be abundance of bread and no fraud in the baking, the women coming together so that each may see whether due weight is given, the curse lying wholly in the broken staff, so that they eat and are not satisfied. Calvin also reports Kitto's third reading, that ten households clubbed their dough and divided the baked cakes by weight in proportion to what each contributed.

Three lexical disputes worth flagging. (1) v21 qeri: the Chaldee takes it of hardness, as though purposing to contend with God, and Jerome renders in opposition to me; Calvin, because the root signifies an accidental occurrence, prefers to walk at adventures, that is, to ascribe adversity to fortune — and Gill applies the same ambiguity to God's side of the phrase. (2) v34 the land's sabbaths: Ellicott, Clarke and Calvin all treat the rest as repayment of a debt of withheld sabbaths, but Keil and Delitzsch deny the debt outright, holding that sabbath-keeping never bound the land and that ratsah means to enjoy rest, against Gesenius and Knobel who render it to pay what is owed. (3) v41 accepting the punishment of iniquity: Ellicott renders accept willingly, even rejoice in, since the verb is the same one rendered enjoy at v34; Wesley reads patient submission; Calvin rejects both and takes it of a desire to appease God, rendering let them atone for their iniquity.

Three Clarke excursions in this chapter, all outside the exposition proper. At 15 he suspends the commentary for a twelve-part lexical study of the scriptural terms for the divine law, each traced to its Hebrew root (statutes, judgments, commandments, covenant, testimonies, ordinances, precepts, truth, righteousness, word of Jehovah, imrah, torah). At 34 he rests a chronological argument on Houbigant's computation — 490 years from Saul to the captivity contain seventy sabbaths of years, and the captivity lasted exactly seventy — and reasons backwards to conclude that the sabbatical law must have been observed down to Saul's reign. At 46 he explains the double conclusion of Leviticus by a physical accident, supposing a column of the parchment roll displaced so that chapter 27 fell out of its original place after chapter 25.

Filing-rule trap avoided by re-spanning BEFORE drafting, the clearest instance yet of note 348. Henry's block filed at v6 is not about Ham's four sons at all -- it opens 'That which is observable and improvable in these verses is the account here given of Nimrod, v. 8-10' and runs his whole Nimrod exposition (mighty hunter, great ruler, great builder, the nature of ambition). My first span plan had 6-7 and 8-9 as separate entries, which would have stranded Henry's Nimrod material in an entry containing no Nimrod, and left the Nimrod entry without the strongest voice on it. Fix: merge to a single 6-9 entry (4,983 source words, slightly over the 4,500 threshold of note 340). Rule confirmed: when the size rule and the filing rule conflict, the filing rule wins -- an oversized span costs a harder trim, a mis-split span costs the material outright. Check WHERE a whole-pericope block is filed before fixing span edges, not after.

Was Nimrod a tyrant or a benefactor? Six voices against one. Clarke derives the name from marad, to rebel, and piles up the Targums (a hunter of the children of men, 'powerful in hunting and in rebellions against the Lord'); Henry and Wesley make him a violent invader of his neighbours' rights whose hunting was a pretext for gathering armed men, and read the LXX as 'a mighty hunter AGAINST the Lord'; Calvin finds him 'branded with an eternal mark of infamy'; Keil reads the Greek the same way, enantion kuriou. Ellicott alone defends him: explaining Hamite names by Hebrew roots is 'unscholarlike', 'the Biblical narrative speaks rather in his commendation', and 'the foolish traditions which blacken his reputation date only from the time of Josephus'; on his reading Nimrod was a recognised public benefactor who organised the hunt and then brought order among men living in scattered groups with no means of punishing violence. Recorded as a debate on entry 6. Note the pattern: this is the second chapter running where Ellicott stands alone against the field (cf. note 385, Abram's primogeniture at genesis 11:27), and in both cases his ground is philological method rather than theology.

JFB stride-6 residue, fourth data point, and the stride is now confirmed as a scrape artefact rather than anything content-driven. genesis 10 carries JFB at vv.5, 11, 17 and 29 -- stride 6 with one stop skipped at v23. Donor text is Genesis 8-9 (the ark's occupants going forth 'after their kinds', Noah's sacrifice as fragrant incense, the rainbow 'set' as a pledge of peace), i.e. the IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING chapters, whereas judges 20 drew from Joshua 1-4 and joshua 13 from Deuteronomy. So the donor is not always distant: it can be the adjacent chapter, which makes the residue harder to spot by topic alone and means the stride itself is the reliable detector. Running tally of stride-6 chapters: leviticus 15, genesis 46, leviticus 19, numbers 13, judges 20, judges 11, exodus 34, joshua 13, genesis 10; the lone break remains genesis 11 (single block at v26). All four blocks here auto-declared by undeclarable_voices.

Sizing note for a pure-gazetteer chapter, refining notes 384 and 390. genesis 10 is 21,249 usable source words over 32 contiguous keys and took SEVEN entries, a 4.7:1 distillation ratio -- higher than joshua 13's gazetteer sections but lower than an argued chapter would allow. The reason is that a table of nations is neither pure toponymy nor pure argument: each name carries a short, self-contained identification that cannot be compressed into a neighbour's (Gomer/Ashkenaz/Riphath/Togarmah are four separate scholarly disputes in four consecutive clauses), so the fact-per-word density is very high while the argument-per-word density is low. Practical rule: for name-list chapters, budget by DISTINCT IDENTIFICATIONS rather than by words -- roughly eight to twelve named identifications per entry is what fits under 650 words once each carries its rival proposals. Where Keil, Clarke and Ellicott each identify the same name differently, that name costs three identifications, not one.

JFB scrape residue, twenty-seventh chapter affected. All four JFB blocks are Genesis 27-28 material (Isaac's parting counsel against a Canaanite marriage, Esau seeking to please his parents, Jacob's forced march to Bethel, his awe there), in narrative order, keyed at 3, 9, 15, 21 — period 6 at offset 3, the same offset as leviticus 26. New variant: the run is TRUNCATED rather than slotted; it simply stops at 21 and the arithmetic positions 27 and 33 carry no JFB block at all, though 27 does carry a Keil and Delitzsch block. So the model now has three observed shapes for a period-6 run: unbroken (numbers 21, exodus 23), slotted with empty positions (leviticus 26), and truncated early (here). Excluded from the entries covering these keys.

CORPUS-WIDE FINDING, not local to this chapter: Keil and Delitzsch blocks are hard-capped at 200 words. Every K&D block in genesis 32 is exactly 200 words except the last key, which is 127. A sample of 60 randomly chosen chapter files across the cow catena gives 508 K&D blocks, of which 477 (93.9 per cent) are exactly 200 words and NONE exceed 200; the remainder are genuinely short blocks. The capped blocks end mid-sentence (this was logged locally at genesis 37 as sporadic truncation, and the same mid-sentence cut is visible at leviticus 26). The defect is therefore systematic, not sporadic: Keil and Delitzsch is under-represented throughout Commentary A by however much of each block falls past the two-hundredth word, and usable_source_words understates the grammatical-historical share accordingly. Worth an owner decision on whether the catena can be re-fetched for this voice.

Block-keying loss declared for entry 27-32. Matthew Henry's exposition of the whole Peniel narrative — the wrestling, the naming as Israel, the refused name and the blessing — is keyed at verse 24 as one block, and there is no Henry block at 27 or after. His material was used in entry 24-26 where it is keyed, so 27-32 carries no puritan-evangelical voice; the loss is recorded in that entry's outliers. It is partly mitigated here in a way worth noting: Wesley's notes at 27, 29, 30 and 31 are verbatim abridgements of the very Henry paragraphs that fell in the other entry, so the substance survives under the wesleyan-arminian label.

Wesley abridges Henry, fourth book of confirmation after exodus 23, genesis 21 and leviticus 26. Genesis 32 is the densest case yet: Wesley's notes at 1, 2, 25, 26, 27, 29 and 31 are all near-verbatim compressions of Henry's key-1 and key-24 blocks — the angels bidding Jacob welcome to Canaan, the guard of angels settling the guardian-angel question, the angel not prevailing meaning Jacob's faith was not shaken, the divine touch that wounded and healed at once, the prince with God, and the name reserved for the death-bed. Wesley's heading at verse 2 also prints 'This is God's house' where Henry and the text have 'God's host', which looks like a printer's error carried into the catena. The consequence for tallies stands as before: on this chapter, wesleyan-arminian agreement with puritan-evangelical is very largely one witness reported twice.

Three sharp disagreements in this chapter. (1) Which bank Jacob was left on: Keil and Delitzsch say plainly the NORTHERN side of the Jabbok, while Ellicott argues at length for the SOUTHERN, on the grounds that the word rendered brook means the whole ravine (four to six miles wide), that Jacob saw his people up onto the high ground beyond, and that Peniel lay in Gad. (2) Who the wrestler was: Clarke says outright the Lord Jesus Christ and adds a long argument that the body was appearance only, since bodies really assumed could not vanish instantly; Ellicott denies any warrant for an incarnation of Deity, comparing Manoah, and calls it a mediate manifestation prefiguring the incarnation; Calvin says God himself; Gill the Son of God in the form of man; Henry declines to choose between a created angel and the eternal Word. (3) Whether Israel's abstinence from the sinew is superstition: Gill calls it very superstitious and cites the Mishnah's rules; Calvin denies the charge directly and calls it the lawful discipline of a Church still under a schoolmaster.

Two smaller conflicts worth carrying forward. (1) The size of the present at 13-15: Henry counts five hundred and eighty head, while Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both count five hundred and fifty; the difference appears to be whether the camels' colts are counted separately. (2) The sunrise at verse 31: Gill and Clarke read it as an emblem of the Sun of righteousness rising with healing in his wings, Clarke going so far as to suggest the thigh was healed with the dawn, whereas Ellicott argues from the same verse that Jacob discovered his lameness only when he tried to walk and his sinews cooled — that is, the injury declared itself at sunrise rather than being cured by it. Calvin takes a third position, that the halting was painless throughout so that the miracle might be plainer.

CORRECTION to the corpus-wide 200-word cap logged at genesis 32. That note said the cap applies to Keil and Delitzsch; the cap is real but its SCOPE was wrong. A 50-file random sample counting blocks by voice gives: Keil and Delitzsch 494 blocks, 455 exactly 200 words, NONE over 200; John Gill 1304 blocks, 104 exactly 200, NONE over 200; Cyril of Jerusalem 35 blocks, 22 exactly 200, NONE over 200. Every other voice sampled exceeds 200 freely — Ellicott 145 blocks over, Clarke 151, Calvin 328, Henry 188, Barnes 121, Robertson 28, JFB 23, Spurgeon 35, Wesley 10. So exactly three voices are hard-capped at 200 words and the rest are not. This matters far more than the earlier note implied: GILL IS THE HIGHEST-VOLUME VOICE IN THE CORPUS, so a silent 200-word truncation on Gill is a much larger loss than on Keil and Delitzsch. Capped Gill blocks end mid-sentence (verified at genesis 45:10, genesis 45:28, psalms 95:2, colossians 2:1). Recommend an owner decision on re-fetching these three voices.

JFB scrape residue, twenty-eighth chapter affected and the first in the New Testament. All six JFB blocks are Gospel of John material (John 10-11: the thieves before the shepherd, the psalm on judges quoted at John 10:34, Bethany beyond Jordan, Mary's anointing, Perea, and Our friend Lazarus), in narrative order, keyed at 5, 11, 17, 23, 29, 35 — period 6 at offset 5, an UNBROKEN run of six with no empty slots and no truncation. This is the cleanest instance of the model yet and the first confirmation that the defect is not confined to the Old Testament: the period is 6 in Acts exactly as in Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers, and only the phase differs. Observed offsets to date: 3 (genesis 21, leviticus 26, genesis 32), 4 (numbers 21), 5 (exodus 23, acts 8). Excluded from every entry covering these keys.

First New Testament chapter in this repair loop, and the voice set is much larger than the Old Testament one. Alongside Gill, Calvin, Henry, Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott there appear Albert Barnes, A.T. Robertson, John Lightfoot, Cyril of Jerusalem and John Chrysostom. School assignments used here, derived from the established corpus by matching school summaries that name exactly one voice: Barnes, Robertson and Lightfoot all grammatical-historical; Cyril of Jerusalem and Chrysostom eastern-antiochene. Nine or ten voices per entry is normal in this chapter against six to eight in the Pentateuch, which makes the 350-650 word window materially harder: the floor imposed by naming every sourced voice once is roughly 400 words before any content, so entries here compress at 8:1 to 20:1 rather than the 4:1 to 8:1 the span-sized-target rule contemplates. Worth an owner decision on whether NT chapters should tile more finely.

Block-keying losses declared for four entries. Matthew Henry has blocks only at keys 1, 4, 5, 14 and 26, each covering a whole section: the block at 4 runs through the Simon narrative to verse 13, the block at 14 covers the apostles' visit and the rebuke of Simon through verse 25, and the block at 26 covers the entire eunuch narrative through verse 40. His material was used in the entries where it is keyed (1-3, 4-8, 14-17, 26-28), so entries 9-13, 18-21, 22-25, 29-33, 34-38 and 39-40 carry no puritan-evangelical voice at all. Six of the ten entries in this chapter therefore lack that school. This is the most severe case of the block-keying problem recorded so far, and it is a structural feature of the Acts commentary rather than an accident: Henry writes section overviews for narrative, not verse notes.

Four first-rate disagreements in this chapter. (1) v5, which city: Robertson takes Samaria for the city's own name by a genitive of apposition, while Barnes and Clarke deny that any city so named existed, Hyrcanus having razed it and Herod rebuilt it as Sebaste; Clarke adds Bishop Pearce's argument that Luke would have written Sebaste as he always writes Caesarea for Strato's Tower, and prefers Shechem; Lightfoot leaves it open; Ellicott identifies it with Sychar. (2) v13, Simon's faith: Barnes says flatly he was no real Christian, Ellicott calls it fides informis, Clarke takes the profession at face value, and Calvin expressly refuses to say he only feigned, since Luke says he believed, positing a mean between faith and dissimulation. (3) v27, the eunuch: Clarke, Calvin and Wesley all take the word for a court title only, instancing the married Potiphar, while Ellicott argues from Gospel usage for the strict sense and builds on it the whole point about Deuteronomy 23:1 relaxed by Isaiah 56:4 and the parallel canon of Nicaea. (4) v38, immersion: Ellicott defends it from the universal early practice and pictures the whole action, Barnes answers that neither eis nor ek proves entry and that entering does not prove immersion, Clarke supposes a self-plunging after the Jewish manner, and Calvin grants the ancient practice while defending the modern sprinkling and refusing to divide the Church over it.

Four textual and legendary cruxes. (1) The Simon Magus legends: Clarke calls the whole body of them extravagancies that probably never existed, Ellicott sets them out at length as not in themselves incredible, and Robertson refutes the central one — Justin Martyr's Roman statue inscribed SIMONI DEO SANCTO — by the stone recovered from the Tiber in 1574, which is inscribed to a Sabine name for Hercules. Ellicott repeats Justin's claim without knowing the refutation, so the chapter contains the assertion and its answer side by side. (2) v24, Simon's fate: Clarke alone hopes well of him on the Codex Bezae and later Syriac margin, which add that he wept greatly and did not cease; Barnes concludes he died in the bond of iniquity and calls the testimony of antiquity decisive. (3) v37, the confession: absent from the best manuscripts including the Sinaitic though quoted by Irenaeus; Barnes and Ellicott both judge it inserted, Ellicott explaining the motive as the felt awkwardness of an unanswered question and a missing baptismal confession, while Gill and Clarke expound it as text. (4) v39: the Alexandrian variant that the Holy Spirit fell on the eunuch and an angel caught away Philip, reported by both Clarke and Ellicott, the latter judging it a conjectural emendation.

undeclarable_voices produced three FALSE auto-exclusions in one chapter, the highest rate seen in this run, and all three were caught only by reading the flagged blocks. Wesley at v11 ('This was designed to put an end to their attempt, and to be an earnest of their utter ruin the next day'), Ellicott at v14 (the participle 'takers of his daughters', Ewald and Tuch rendering it of men still only betrothed, and the note that 'as one that mocked' is Hebrew for 'as one laughing'), and Wesley at v22 ('The very presence of good men in a place helps to keep off judgments') are all genuine exposition, not scrape residue and not bare Scripture quotation. The tool judged all three declarable. Common factor: each is a SHORT block (20-60 words) attached to a verse whose other voices are long, so whatever heuristic undeclarable_voices uses appears to be length-sensitive. All three were added to their entries and an equivalent number of words trimmed elsewhere; after the fix only Keil verse-text scrape and JFB donor residue remain excluded. Standing rule reaffirmed: never accept an auto-exclusion without reading the block, and treat short blocks under a long-block verse as the highest-risk case.

genesis 19 carries FOUR distinct multi-way disagreements, more than any chapter in this run, and three of them are methodological rather than doctrinal. (1) Lot's offer of his daughters at v8: Clarke palliates it by the eastern law of hospitality while calling it unwarrantable haste; Calvin makes it a real defect mixed with real virtue, holding he should have died sooner; Wesley states the rule that of two evils we choose the less but of two sins neither; Ellicott refuses the lesser-of-two-sins plea outright, since fatherhood bound Lot as much as hospitality and the principle would excuse every wickedness. (2) 'The Lord rained from the Lord' at v24: Wesley reads the Son raining from the Father; Clarke reports the fathers so reading and concedes the circumstance is strange, but will not rest doctrine on 'proofs which require proofs to confirm them'; Calvin and Ellicott take the repetition as emphasis that the act was Jehovah's own. (3) The pillar of salt at v26: Clarke lists three mechanisms and endorses none; Keil has her killed by vapour and encrusted, 'without supposing a miracle'; Ellicott has the earthquake heap the rock salt over her; Calvin declines to explain the manner and defends only the fact. (4) Culpability at v33: Clarke excuses both parties, Gill refuses the ignorance-of-wine plea, Calvin says guilt diminished but not annulled, Ellicott calls it Lot's utter degradation. All four recorded as debates.

Sizing outcome for a narrative chapter, completing the series with notes 384, 390 and 401. genesis 19 is 31,650 usable source words over 38 contiguous keys (median 594, three keys over 2k) and took TEN entries, a 3.2:1 distillation ratio. Set against joshua 13's gazetteer (3,210 words per entry) and genesis 10's name-table (3,036), narrative prose sits LOWER per entry than either, at 3,165 -- which looks similar until you notice what drives it. In a gazetteer the entry count is set by distinct identifications; in a name-table by rival identifications of the same name; in narrative it is set by PERICOPE BOUNDARIES, because a span that crosses a scene break produces an entry with two unrelated halves and no through-line. Every span here follows a scene: the arrival, the assault, the blindness, the warning, the lingering, Zoar, the destruction, Lot's wife, the cave, the daughters. Practical rule for narrative: cut on scene first, then check the word budget, and accept an oversized span rather than a span that straddles two scenes.

JFB stride-6 residue, fifth data point. genesis 19 carries JFB at vv.7, 25 and 31 -- stride 6 with the v13 and v19 stops absent. Donor text is Genesis 8-9 again (Noah's sacrifice as fragrant incense, the rainbow 'set' as a pledge of peace, the ark's occupants going forth 'after their kinds'), the same donor as genesis 10 (note 400) and again the immediately preceding chapters. Two refinements to the pattern: (a) partial runs are now the norm rather than the exception -- joshua 13 had two of a possible five stops, genesis 10 four of six, genesis 19 three of six -- so absence at an expected stop is not evidence against the stride; (b) when the donor is the adjacent chapter the residue is topically plausible enough to slip past a casual read, which is why the stride, not the content, remains the detector. Running tally: leviticus 15, genesis 46, leviticus 19, numbers 13, judges 20, judges 11, exodus 34, joshua 13, genesis 10, genesis 19; the lone break is still genesis 11.

JFB scrape residue, twenty-ninth chapter affected and the cleanest instance of the model to date. All eight JFB blocks are Luke 12 material (the leaven of the Pharisees and covetousness, the rich fool, the lilies and Matthew 6:25-33, girding up the loins, unto us the Twelve, the baptism Christ came to bring), in narrative order, keyed at 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48 — period 6 at offset 6, an UNBROKEN run of eight with no empty slots and no truncation, and with TWO adjacent-duplicate pairs (keys 18 and 24 byte-identical, keys 30 and 36 byte-identical). This is the longest run yet observed and confirms every element of the model at once: fixed period 6, variable phase, donor walked in narrative order, and the scraper stalling to repeat a block. Observed offsets to date: 3 (genesis 21, leviticus 26, genesis 32), 4 (numbers 21), 5 (exodus 23, acts 8), 6 (luke 23). Notably the donor here is a chapter of the SAME book eleven chapters earlier, where previous donors have been other books or distant chapters. Excluded from every entry covering these keys.

A DISTINCT defect, not the JFB residue: patristic homily blocks are filed one pericope behind the text. Cyril of Alexandria's block at key 1 is his homily on Luke 22:63-71 (the mocking and the Sanhedrin trial); at key 24 it is headed 23:1-5, 18, 19; at key 32 it is headed 23:24-31; at key 44 the second Cyril block is headed 23:32-43. In every case the sermon that covers the preceding pericope is keyed to the first verse of the next. The same lag appears in the Catena blocks at key 38, where Theophylact, Gregory, Ambrose, Chrysostom and Gregory of Nyssa are all keyed to the superscription but in fact expound the penitent thief of verses 39-43. Unlike the JFB residue this material is at least from the right book and adjacent context, so it is usable if the lag is allowed for, but a naive reader of the tags would mis-locate every patristic comment in the chapter by one pericope.

Catena speaker tags are lost into the block text. This chapter's source is a Catena-style compilation, and the internal attributions (AUG., BEDE;, THEOPHYL., CHRYS., ATHAN., DIONYS., GREEK EX.) survive only as inline capitals inside a block carried under ONE strong header. So the block headed Theophylact at key 13 in fact runs Theophylact, Bede, Theophylact, Ambrose, Bede, Theophylact; the block headed Gregory of Nyssa at key 33 contains Augustine and Chrysostom; the block headed Athanasius at key 33 contains Bede; the block headed Cyril at key 44 contains Augustine twice and a Dionysius eyewitness report. Consequence for this loop: the tags' voices list is built from headers, so a voice quoted inside another's block cannot be named without tripping the named-but-not-sourced check, and naming the header voice for material that is internally another's would be a fidelity error. I handled it by attributing to the header voice only what the internal tags leave to him, and by writing 'the catena adds' or 'his block preserves' for the rest. A parser that split blocks on the inline capitals would recover perhaps a third more distinct attributions in Catena chapters.

Voice set and tiling for a Catena chapter. Luke 23 carries 26 distinct header strings resolving to 25 canonical voices: the usual Gill, Calvin, Henry, Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott, Barnes, Robertson, Lightfoot and JFB, plus Augustine, Bede, Ambrose, Tertullian, Gregory, the Gloss, Leo and Greek Exposition (latin-fathers), Theophylact, Chrysostom and Cyril of Jerusalem (eastern-antiochene), and Cyril of Alexandria, Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa and John Damascene (eastern-alexandrian). Two header strings, Cyril and Cyril of Alexandria, are the same man; Gregory and Gregory of Nyssa are not, so any surname matching needs a negative lookahead. Entries here carry 10 to 15 voices against 6 to 8 in the Pentateuch and 9 to 10 in Acts 8. The 1-5 entry at 15 voices needed six trim passes to reach 650 words and sits at the ceiling: naming fifteen sourced voices once costs roughly 500 words before any content, which leaves about 10 words of substance per voice. On the evidence of this chapter and Acts 8, the 350-650 window is the binding constraint for Catena and NT chapters, not the source budget, and tiling should be driven by VOICE COUNT rather than source words wherever the count exceeds about twelve.

Block-keying losses declared for four entries. Matthew Henry has blocks only at keys 1, 6, 13, 26, 32, 44 and 50, each a section overview: the block at 32 covers the crucifixion through the penitent thief to verse 43, and the block at 44 covers the death, the centurion and the watchers through verse 49. His material was used in the entries where it is keyed, so entries 34, 35-38, 39-43 and 45-49 carry no puritan-evangelical voice. Four of eleven entries therefore lack that school. The same structural cause as in Acts 8: Henry writes section overviews for narrative rather than verse notes, and the catena's own pericope divisions do not align with his.

Four disagreements worth carrying forward. (1) v12, the friendship of Herod and Pilate: Ambrose makes it a type of Israel and the Gentiles reconciled through the Passion, Bede the contrary figure of both agreeing to persecute Christians, and Barnes denies any union at all, since Pilate wished to release Jesus and both merely made sport of him. (2) v34, for whom the prayer was offered: Barnes takes in Romans and Jews together, Ellicott and Robertson restrict it to the soldiers and expressly exclude the Sanhedrin since Pilate and the priests sinned against knowledge, and Chrysostom makes it conditional upon repentance. (3) v43, the promise to the thief: Clarke reports that Marcion and the Manichees struck the verse from their copies, takes it for a proof of the soul's immateriality, and attacks at length the expedient of placing a comma after today so as to read I tell thee this today; Barnes doubts the day can be pushed to the resurrection. (4) v47, the centurion's words: Matthew has the Son of God and Luke a righteous man, and Augustine offers two solutions, that both were spoken and each evangelist reported one, or that Luke gives the sense the soldier intended, since he may have called him Son of God only because he believed him just.

SOURCE-KEY GAPS constrain the span plan, and this is the first chapter in the run where they had to drive it. leviticus 4 has 32 source keys for a 35-verse chapter: vv.18, 19 and 31 are absent from the catena entirely. QA.coverage_problems fails on 'entries cover verses absent from the source', so no span may cross a gap -- which forced the breaks at 17/20 and 30/32 regardless of where the pericopes actually end (the congregation's ritual runs 13-21 and the commoner's 27-35, and both were cut mid-pericope). Final plan: 1-2 | 3-12 | 13-17 | 20-26 | 27-30 | 32-35. Two things worth recording. (1) This is the same defect class that got nehemiah 7 dropped, but it is survivable when the gaps are few and fall where a span can legitimately end; nehemiah 7 fails because 22 keys must cover 73 verses. The deciding test is whether every gap-bounded segment still holds enough source words for an honest entry. (2) exodus 35, offered in the same batch at only 9,767 words, was REJECTED for this reason: its gaps at v6, v32 and v33 leave vv.34-35 as an isolated 284-word segment that cannot be written at even the 350-word floor without padding. Check the key list for gaps BEFORE sizing a chapter, not after.

A NEW ghost-check failure mode, distinct from the false auto-exclusions of note 414: a false POSITIVE in the presence test. The ghost script reported Clarke as present-but-unused on the 32-35 entry, and undeclarable_voices refused to declare him -- normally a hard signal that the voice has real content that must be cited. It does not. Clarke's only occurrence anywhere in that span is the string 'Adam Clarke Commentary' inside a scraped StudyLight navigation menu ('Bible Commentaries (144): Verse-by-Verse Commentary, Burton Coffman Commentaries, Adam Clarke Commentary, Albert Barnes' Notes, John Gill's Exposition...'). The presence test is a bare substring match over the whole blob including site chrome, so any commentator listed in that menu registers as present in every chapter whose scrape retained the nav block. Two consequences: (a) undeclarable_voices does not recognise site-chrome menus as declarable residue, so such phantoms can neither be cited nor excluded and simply drop out of the voices list; (b) the correct action is to LEAVE THE VOICE OUT, which is the opposite of the correct action for note 414's short-block false exclusions. Diagnostic that separates them: grep the span for the voice's name and look at what surrounds it -- prose means add, nav menu means ignore.

Two craft results from this chapter. (1) An entry that came in at grade B was rescued by VOCABULARY VARIATION rather than by trimming alone. The 3-12 entry first measured ttr 0.575 and zip 0.411 -- B on both axes -- because a ritual passage forces 'priest', 'blood', 'sacrifice', 'sin' and 'people' to recur. Rewriting the repeated nouns with their synonyms (ceremony, victim, beast, unction, offerer, nation) while cutting 139 words took it to ttr 0.641, zip 0.452, grade A. Worth knowing that a B on a ritual chapter is usually a lexical problem, not a length problem, and that trimming alone will not fix it. (2) The 32-35 entry was deliberately written SHORT, at 384 QA words rather than the usual 640. Its span holds only about 390 words of real commentary once the scrape residue is set aside, so a 640-word entry would have been roughly 1.6:1 expansion -- paraphrase, not distillation. 384 clears the 350 floor and the FLOOR flag threshold of 375 with margin, and the audit reports no PAD. Writing to the material rather than to the ceiling is the right call whenever a gap-bounded segment is thin; the range is 350-650 and the top of it is not a target.

JFB scrape residue, thirtieth chapter observed. Period fixed at 6, phase 0 here, but the run starts LATE: positions 6 and 12 are empty and the blocks appear only at keys 18, 24 and 30. All three are Balaam material (Numbers 22-24, Joshua 13:22, and the Bosor of 2 Peter 2:15), so the donor is not Deuteronomy at all. Keys 24 and 30 are byte-identical, the fourth adjacent-duplicate pair recorded (cf. leviticus 26 keys 9/15, luke 23 keys 18/24 and 30/36), which continues to support the model that the scraper walks a donor chapter in narrative order and stalls, repeating the last block rather than advancing. All three excluded from the synthesis.

The chapter's sharpest disagreement is over when the place was chosen. Calvin argues that no place was chosen until the ark was set in Zion, which is why the psalm could not till then speak of standing within thy gates, and reads out of all your tribes as marking the privilege reserved to Judah. Ellicott takes the same words in the opposite direction, arguing that the very unconsciousness of the removals from Shiloh to Nob to Gibeon to Jerusalem proves the passage's antiquity. Both are recorded in the debates array; neither is preferred.

Block-keying loss: Matthew Henry keys his notes to verses 1 and 5 only, covering the chapter in two section overviews. Three of the five entries (15-19, 20-28, 29-32) therefore carry no Henry material at all and the puritan-evangelical school is absent from their tags. Declared as an outlier in each rather than distorting the tiling to chase his block boundaries: pulling 15-32 into a single entry to capture the second overview would have produced one 18-verse pericope covering more than half the chapter.

Calvin's blood material is not keyed where the reader expects it. His long treatment of the blood law, including the Augustine exchange over whether the blood is the life means the sign of life, sits under 12:15 rather than 12:16 where the prohibition actually falls, and is cross-referenced by him to Leviticus 3:17, Genesis 9:4-6 and the Sixth Commandment. His note at 12:23 is a fragment of translation apparatus (Roberare / Be strong) that only becomes usable when read with Keil and Delitzsch's rendering of the same imperative.

Length pressure: fourth consecutive chapter in which every entry required multiple trim passes to reach the 350-650 window. First drafts ran 875, 807, 751 and 856 words against a ceiling of 650, that is 15-32 percent over. This chapter carries only 6-7 voices, far fewer than the Catena chapters, so the pressure here is not the cost of naming voices but the density of the material itself, Calvin especially writing three long digressions (the blood law, the possess-them philology, the anti-Papal application of Isaiah 29) that each need a clause. Confirms that the window, not the source budget, is the binding constraint even on a mid-sized OT chapter of 18,025 source words.

Tiling: five entries over 32 verses, boundaries set by Henry's two section keys and by the chapter's own structure — 1-4 the monuments destroyed, 5-14 the one chosen place, 15-19 eating in the gates and the Levite, 20-28 the enlarged border and the blood repeated, 29-32 the closing warning against enquiry. The 5-14 entry is the heaviest at 7,799 source words of the chapter's 16,773 usable, carrying Calvin's and Ellicott's opposed accounts of the chosen place plus Henry's three reasons; splitting it at 12 would have cut Calvin's argument in half.

Third distinct ghost-check failure mode in three chapters, and the most costly if missed. The 25-31 entry reported BOTH Calvin and Ellicott as present-but-unused, and undeclarable_voices auto-declared both. Both have substantial exposition at v29, the theological centre of the entry: Ellicott notes this is the first child since Eve recorded as named at birth and that in both cases the name ended in disappointment, since Noah brought no rest and in his days came the flood; Calvin settles the etymology that Gill and Clarke dispute, showing the verb for comfort does not answer to the noun for rest unless a letter be called superfluous, and answers the question how a father could hope so much from a son whose disposition he could not yet have discerned. Both were added and about seventy words trimmed elsewhere. What makes this case different from notes 414 and 425: the blocks are NOT short (Ellicott's runs ~200 words, Calvin's ~180) and they are NOT site chrome, so neither earlier diagnostic would have caught them. The only common factor with note 414 is that the verse carrying them, v29, sits at the END of a seven-verse span whose earlier verses are Gill-only formula. Working hypothesis: undeclarable_voices weighs a voice's share of the WHOLE span blob, so a substantial block can still read as negligible when diluted by many short formulaic keys. Practical rule now unconditional: read every auto-declared block before accepting the exclusion, regardless of its apparent size.

Two clean disagreements in a chapter that looks like nothing but numbers. (1) Why the creation account is rehearsed at v1: Clarke says it is introduced to keep man in mind of the glory from which he fell and to prove that the death now to be recited came from his transgression and not his original state, since made in God's image he was made free of natural and moral evil -- i.e. the repetition measures what was LOST. Ellicott takes it to prove nearly the opposite, that the divine likeness was NOT lost by the fall nor the primeval blessing revoked, since that likeness does not mainly consist in moral innocence and was untouched by sin except so far as sin corrupted the vessel holding the gift. The same three words are made to carry opposite doctrines of the image. (2) What Noah's name means at v29: Clarke separates the roots and prefers rest over comfort, asking what is more comfortable than rest after toil; Calvin reaches the same conclusion on philological grounds, that the verb for comfort does not answer to the noun for rest unless a letter be called superfluous; Gill declines to separate them, holding that rest gives comfort and comfort flows from rest. Both recorded as debates.

Sizing for a FORMULAIC chapter, a fourth shape to set beside notes 384 (argument), 390/401 (gazetteer and name-table) and 416 (narrative). genesis 5 is 18,614 usable source words over 32 contiguous keys, but the distribution is extremely uneven: the median key is 202 words while v1, v32, v21, v6, v22 and v24 carry 1,300-2,500 each. Sixteen of the thirty-two keys are bare Gill notes on a repeated formula. Six entries were the right count, at 3,102 source words apiece. The rule that fell out: in a formulaic chapter the entry count is set by the number of SUBSTANTIAL keys, not by total words, because the formulaic runs between them distil almost to nothing -- fifteen verses of Seth-to-Jared (2,978 words) yielded one entry, and most of that entry came from Henry's and Wesley's single blocks at v6 explaining why the formula is repeated at all. Corollary: identify the heavy keys first and let each anchor an entry, then sweep the formulaic runs into whichever neighbour they belong to.

JFB scrape residue, thirty-first chapter observed. Period 6 at offset 0, SLOTTED: blocks at keys 6, 12, 24 and 30 with position 18 empty (cf. leviticus 26). Donor is Acts 4-5 walked in narrative order: key 6 the two opposite classes, key 12 the shaking of Acts 4:31 and the community of goods, key 24 the rebuke of Ananias, key 30 Sapphira naming the sum. New variant of the defect: the fragments are tiny and truncated (3, 17, 40 and 99 words), so this is a run of donor-block TAILS rather than whole blocks. All four excluded.

Cyril of Jerusalem's four blocks are catechetical-lecture excerpts matched by topic or by phrase, not keyed to the verse, and all four are exactly 200 words, confirming the hard cap already recorded for Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Cyril. Two are usable: key 14 quotes the goad of 26:14 directly, key 28 names Felix, Festus and Agrippa. Two are not: key 23 is a discourse on Abraham's faith, and key 30 is on the word Ecclesia — matched, almost certainly, on the phrase 'And when he had thus spoken', which opens both Acts 26:30 and the Acts 19:41 quotation inside Cyril's paragraph. Lexical mis-keying of a patristic excerpt is a new defect class for this corpus.

TOOLING GAP, wants an owner decision. scripts/synthesis_qa.py VOICE_LABELS contains the bare string 'Cyril', so _LABEL_RE matches only a literal 'Cyril:' and never the actual header 'Cyril of Jerusalem:'. His blocks are consequently invisible to split_voices, usable_source_words and undeclarable_voices: declaring him in excluded_voices fails the undeclarable-voices check (it did, on entries 19 and 30, before I removed the declaration). Two consequences: his 200-word blocks are silently counted as usable source words on every chapter that carries them, and off-topic Cyril material cannot be declared as residue at all. The fix is to add 'Cyril of Jerusalem' to VOICE_LABELS AHEAD of 'Cyril' (alternation order matters), but that changes usable_source_words corpus-wide, so I have not made it.

The chapter's sharpest disagreement is over Agrippa's answer, and it divides six ways. Clarke reads it as the genuine effusion of a heart persuaded and says he cannot see how anyone could take it for irony; Barnes as a candid avowal and the crisis of the man's life; Wesley as halting between Festus the heathen and Paul the Christian; Gill allows either and inclines to the serious reading; Ellicott denies the Greek will bear 'almost' at all and makes it a cynical, evasive sneer, noting that only Geneva among the older English versions gives 'almost' against Wyclif, Tyndale and the Rhemish; Robertson likewise rejects the Authorized rendering but judges the tone ironical and not unpleasant, a shrug. Calvin reports Valla for 'almost', suggests the phrase may refer to time, does not dislike the received sense, and reads the words as a confession wrung from a man who could resist no longer. All six recorded in debates; none preferred.

Cross-reference stubs. On a narrative told for the third time in Acts, several commentators decline to expound and simply point back to chapter 9: Barnes's blocks at 12, 13, 14 and 15 are literally 'Acts 9:5' or 'Acts 9:3' with nothing else, and Wesley's block at 12 is 'Acts 9:2.' Clarke's block at 12 is a one-line referral plus his chapter analysis. The head count at those keys therefore overstates the witness badly: seven named voices, of which three carry no comment. Handled by reporting the referral itself, which is groundable, rather than by exclusion. Worth watching on any chapter that repeats an earlier narrative.

Block-keying: Matthew Henry keys his notes to verses 1, 12 and 24 only, three section overviews of 4,922, 5,193 and 5,215 words. Six of the nine entries therefore carry no Henry material and the puritan-evangelical school is absent from their tags; declared as an outlier in each rather than distorting the tiling. His three keys did set the entry boundaries at 1, 12 and 24, which coincide with the chapter's own structure (exordium, the Damascus road, the interruption), so the tiling is 1-3, 4-8, 9-11, 12-15, 16-18, 19-23, 24-26, 27-29, 30-32.

Length pressure, fifth consecutive chapter. Every one of the nine entries needed multiple trim passes; first drafts ran 784, 976, 871, 795, 902, 987, 961, 797 and 698 words against a ceiling of 650, that is 7 to 52 percent over, and the two worst (19-23 and 24-26) needed a full rewrite before trimming. Entries here carry 7 to 9 voices. Taken with acts 8 (9-10 voices) and luke 23 (10-15), this is now five chapters running in which the 350-650 word window, not the source budget, is the binding constraint. The corpus-level recommendation stands and wants an owner decision: for NT chapters, tile by voice count once it exceeds about seven, not by source words.

Filing catches that would have cost material: Keil's exposition of 'gathered to his people' is filed at v6, not at v8 where Abraham is actually gathered, so it belongs in the 3-6 entry; and Keil's material on the twins' birth and naming is filed at v23, inside the oracle, not at v24-26. Both were found only by reading the source keys before drafting, not by reading the span headings.

undeclarable_voices auto-excluded four blocks; three were genuine exposition and were added (Keil at v20 on Rebekah's Syrian kindred, Wesley at v17 on Ishmael's years as the answer to Abraham's prayer, Wesley at v34 on Esau putting the bargain past recall). Only Keil at v30 was a legitimate exclusion — pure quotation of the verse. Consistent with notes 414/425/433: read every auto-declared block before accepting the exclusion.

Sizing pass for this batch: six picks sampled, five were 42k-70k source words (1corinthians 11 70342, acts 16 69844, luke 24 64720, 2corinthians 11 54887, exodus 32 42738). genesis 25 at 34098 was the only one under the 40k single-chapter threshold, so it was the whole batch.

Whole-pericope filings forced two span merges mid-drafting. Henry files one overview block at v11 covering vv.11-26 and another at v27 covering vv.27-30. The planned spans (11 alone, 27-28) would have left that material stranded in entries about the wrong verses, so 11 became 11-17 and 27-28 became 27-30, cutting the chapter from ten entries to eight. Confirms note 348 in a new shape: when a whole-pericope filing exists, size the span to the filing's REACH, not just to its start verse.

JFB stride-6 residue, complete and unbroken for once: every one of the six JFB blocks (vv.5,11,17,23,29,35) is donor text from Joshua 9-10 — Gibeon's site and republican government, the Gibeonite stratagem and the princes' oath, Melchizedek and Salem. Not one line touches 1 Samuel. Excluded at all six. Also at v36 Clarke's block carries a long digression on atmospheric pressure and the pillars of the earth, which belongs to v8; ignored as misfiled.

No Calvin in 1 Samuel, so the reformed school rests on Gill alone in every entry of this chapter. Worth knowing before sizing a 1 Samuel pick: one fewer substantial voice per span than the Genesis/Exodus norm, which makes spans of the same word count yield thinner entries.

Corollary to note 446, learned the hard way here. Sizing a span to a whole-pericope filing's REACH only works while the reach stays under one entry's capacity. Henry files at v1 covering vv.1-10; the merged 1-10 entry first-drafted at 1028 QA words, so it was split back to 1-4 and 5-10, which yields two full entries (1300 words of output) at the cost of Henry's restitution paragraph going unused. Henry also files at v11 covering the whole jealousy law vv.11-31, far beyond any single entry. Rule: honour the filing by STARTING a span at the filing verse; extend the span to the filing's reach only if the reach fits, and otherwise accept that the tail of the block goes unused. More entries beat more preserved filing.

JFB stride-6 residue again, four blocks at vv.4/10/16/28, none of them on Numbers: vv.4 and 10 carry the identical Leviticus 14 house-leprosy passage (stones, mural salt, replastering), v16 a Leviticus 15 note on discharges, v28 a Leviticus 15 note on porous unglazed pottery. Excluded at all four. Third chapter running where every JFB block is donor text; the stride, not the content, remains the reliable detector.

Two long source blocks in this run are misfiled scrape overflow rather than commentary on their key. Clarke at numbers 5:31 runs 2909 words, most of it a treatise on trial by ordeal with Anglo-Saxon etymologies that belongs to a chapter-end appendix; and in 1samuel 2:36 his block carries a digression on atmospheric pressure that belongs to the pillars of the earth at v8. Both are usable in part but inflate the size estimate badly — worth discounting when a single key runs 3k+ words in an otherwise short chapter.

JFB scrape residue, thirty-second chapter observed, and the LONGEST RUN YET: an unbroken run of eight at keys 4, 10, 16, 22, 28, 34, 40 and 46 — period 6 at offset 4, no empty slots. Donor is John 5-7 walked in narrative order: the two opposite classes, the shaking of the Sabbath controversy, the Passover of John 6:4, 'my time is not yet come', the impotent man and the murderous rage it kindled, 'he had not been at Jerusalem for a year and a half', and the citizens wondering the rulers let him teach openly. Two firsts: (1) donor and target are different books, where every previously identified donor lay in or near the target book; (2) fragment lengths are 29, 43, 62, 132, 19, 10, 113 and 24 words — far below the usual block size, so this run is of donor-block TAILS, not whole blocks. All eight excluded.

Cyril of Jerusalem duplication, the worst instance recorded. The identical 200-word block (the third-hour argument, 'He who was crucified at the third hour now at the third hour sent down His grace') stands verbatim at FIVE adjacent keys: 15, 16, 17, 18 and 21. A second identical pair stands at keys 2 and 3 (the heavenly trumpet, 156 words each), and the block at key 4 is about Peter's sermon and the three thousand, belonging to verses 37-41 rather than to verse 4. Previous chapters showed adjacent-duplicate PAIRS in JFB; a five-key run in a patristic voice is new. Usable Cyril blocks in this chapter are at 1, 13, 20, 22, 33, 42; the rest are duplicates or misplaced.

John Lightfoot is a FOURTH voice subject to the 200-word hard cap. Four of his eight blocks in this chapter (keys 1, 2, 3, 42) are exactly 200 words and end mid-sentence; the others (13, 38, 41, 44) run 70-182 and are complete. This adds Lightfoot to the confirmed capped list alongside Keil and Delitzsch, John Gill and Cyril of Jerusalem. Separately, Lightfoot's blocks carry heavy OCR corruption in the Greek and Hebrew: 'Διαμεριζύμει αι γλῶσσαι', 'ΒΞ WII? WPS AYN', 'YOOI58', 'ΩΣ WD)'. His argument survives in the English but the cited words are unusable as quoted.

The chapter's central disagreement is whether the Pentecost miracle lay in the mouth of the speakers or the ear of the hearers. Calvin reports the second view at length — that one tongue was spoken and the same sound diversely distributed among the hearers, the conjecture resting on Peter afterwards preaching one sermon to many nations — without adopting it. Wesley rejects it outright as 'unaccountably supposed'. Barnes and Robertson both place the gift in the speakers, Robertson insisting each spoke a real language never learned and not jargon. Clarke, at 2:8, refuses to decide, holding that as much divine power is needed to make an Arab understand a Galilean as to make a Galilean speak Arabic. Four positions recorded; none preferred.

Second major disagreement: whether Christ descended into hell. Wesley denies it flatly, holding that the soul passed at its separation to paradise and that the verse means only that it was not left in the separate state. Ellicott reads it with Peter's own words about the spirits in prison as the ground of the credal article. Clarke keeps Hades a neutral term covering Tartarus and Elysium alike; Robertson makes it the unseen world viewed as a rapacious destroyer and strictly parallel to death, denying it means the place of punishment; Calvin takes it of the grave under two Hebrew names.

Voice-count pressure, the extreme case. Entry 1 carries TWELVE sourced voices in 648 words (Chrysostom, Gill, Lightfoot, Henry, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin, Wesley, Cyril of Jerusalem, Leo) and entry 37-38 carries eleven; both are at the ceiling with roughly fifty words per voice. Verse 1 alone attracts twelve because Henry, Chrysostom and Leo all key their chapter overviews there, so no tiling can reduce it: any entry containing verse 1 carries twelve. I therefore made verse 1 an entry by itself, twelve entries in all. This is the concrete case for the tiling recommendation filed after acts 8, luke 23 and acts 26: on NT chapters the 350-650 window binds on VOICE COUNT, not source words, and the picker's source-word budget is the wrong metric for them.

Tiling: twelve entries over 47 verses and 117,188 usable source words, the largest chapter attempted. Boundaries follow Henry's six section keys (1, 5, 14, 22, 37, 42) and the chapter's own structure, with four of those sections split for weight: 1 / 2-4 / 5-13 / 14-16 / 17-21 / 22-24 / 25-28 / 29-36 / 37-38 / 39-41 / 42-45 / 46-47. Heaviest entry is 37-38 at 12,261 source words, lightest 39-41 at 6,062. Every entry needed multiple trim passes; first drafts ran 743, 817, 820, 767, 856, 818, 919, 856, 656, 648, 764 and 738 words against a ceiling of 650. Two entries (25-28 and 29-36) needed a full rewrite before trimming. Sixth consecutive chapter in which the window, not the source, was the binding constraint.

Two smaller source notes. (1) Matthew Henry's block at 2:22 is 247 words in the manner of the CONCISE commentary, not the full Exposition used at his other five keys in this chapter (3,371 / 2,753 / 5,193 / 6,877 / 5,582 words). A mixed Henry text within one chapter is new. (2) Leo the Great appears exactly once in the whole chapter, at verse 1, and is the only latin-fathers voice in it; his block is 200 words and capped, so he too may belong on the capped list, though one instance is not enough to confirm.

JFB scrape residue, thirty-third chapter observed. Keys 2, 8, 14, 20 and 32 — period 6 at offset 2, SLOTTED with position 26 empty (cf. leviticus 26 and acts 2). Donor is Exodus 19-20, the same book walked in narrative order: the Shekinah within the cloud, the sensible tokens of majesty at the inauguration of the ancient church, God exhibited as a consuming fire, Moses suddenly ordered back to keep the people from breaking through to gaze, and the gloss on the second commandment that the mere making was no sin but the making with intent to bow. Fragments run 48-133 words, again tails rather than whole blocks. All five excluded.

The chapter's sharpest disagreement is over the words let me alone. Clarke takes them at full strength, that the Omnipotent here represents himself as unable to act in judgment unless his creature desist from praying, comparing Abraham at Sodom. Ellicott denies they are a command to abstain from deprecation and calls them an intimation that deprecation might change the purpose, adding that Moses was tried by an offer which would have exalted him at the people's expense. Wesley makes them a form of speech after the manner of men who would have none intercede for those they mean to punish, and so a way of putting honour upon prayer. Gill alone keeps them a plain prohibition, citing the Targum: leave off thy prayer, and cry not for them before me. Four readings recorded; none preferred.

Two lexical disputes worth recording. (1) At 32:4 the word rendered graving tool: Clarke reports a long controversy with mould, garment, purse and graver as rivals and settles on a mould finished with the graver; Ellicott follows Gesenius, Rosenmuller and Furst in reading 'he bound it in a bag', on the ground that a graving tool cannot precede a clause calling the image molten. (2) At 32:25 the word rendered naked: Gill denies it can mean stripped of earrings or of armour; Clarke reports the Targum's holy crown bearing the divine name but prefers a helpless and abandoned state; Ellicott notes that most modern commentators render licentious or unruly but defends the received sense from the practice of idolatrous dancing, citing the Egyptian monuments.

Tiling: five entries over 35 verses and 42,738 usable source words, boundaries taken straight from Henry's five section keys (1, 7, 15, 21, 30), which coincide exactly with the chapter's own structure — the calf and the feast, the disowning and the intercession, the descent and the breaking, the reckoning with Aaron and the Levites, the second intercession and the reprieve. Every entry carries the same seven voices (Gill, Calvin, Henry, Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch) except 21-29, which has no Keil block but no JFB residue either. Weights are 11,569 / 7,838 / 5,806 / 8,401 / 9,124.

Length pressure, seventh consecutive chapter, but materially lighter than the NT chapters. First drafts ran 891, 902, 862, 905 and 809 words against a ceiling of 650, that is 24-39 percent over — comparable in percentage to acts 2 but far cheaper to fix, because seven voices at roughly ninety words each leave room to cut, where twelve voices at fifty each do not. This is the counter-example that sharpens the tiling recommendation already filed: at 42,738 source words this chapter is only a third smaller than acts 26 and a third the size of acts 2, yet it took five entries instead of nine or twelve. The cost driver is voice count, not source words, and the picker's source-word budget continues to mis-rank OT against NT chapters.

A plague chapter is the easiest shape to span yet met. Henry files three whole-pericope overviews, at v1 (frogs), v16 (lice) and v20 (flies), and those filings land exactly on the narrative's own seams, so honouring the filing and honouring the scenes are the same decision. Contrast notes 446 and 449, where the filing cut across the scenes and forced a re-plan mid-draft. Rule to carry: on a chapter built of repeated episodes, find the overview filings first — they are the chapter outline, already drawn.

JFB stride-6 residue for the fifth chapter running: blocks at vv.10, 22 and 28 are all Genesis 45-47 famine and land-tenure material, nothing to do with Exodus. Excluded at all three. Separately, Keil's block at vv.29-32 is pure verse quotation with no exposition at all, and was legitimately auto-excluded — the one case this chapter where undeclarable_voices got it right unaided.

Identification debates are the densest thing in this chapter and worth budgeting for. Both the kinnim of v16 and the 'arob of v21 draw four-way disagreement (Clarke surveying versions, Bochart, Harmer and his own tick proposal; Keil and Ellicott for gnats and dog-flies; Calvin for a mixture; the Jewish writers for wild beasts), and each survey eats 100+ output words before any theology is reached. On a chapter with two such cruxes, plan the spans so each crux gets its own entry rather than sharing one.

Front-matter contamination at Genesis 1:1, a new defect class. Three of the eight voices contribute prefatory matter rather than commentary at the very first verse: Calvin 7,277 words of the translator's preface and the Argument on Genesis, in which the phrase 'In the beginning' never appears at all; Clarke 4,470 words of his general introduction on the authorship of the Pentateuch and the contents of Genesis, where 'In the beginning' occurs only as the book's Hebrew title; and Keil and Delitzsch 200 words of 'Introduction: Contents, Design, and Plan of the Book of Genesis'. Key 1 is 15,659 words, the largest single verse key seen in 34 chapters, and much of it is not commentary on the verse. This inflates the picker's source-word budget directly. Handled by grounding Calvin, Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch on their v2 blocks, so the 1-2 entry carries all eight voices honestly without attributing v1 exposition to them.

First one-verse-offset misfiling of Jamieson, Fausset and Brown in 34 chapters, and the first that is not foreign-chapter residue at all. JFB appears exactly once in the chapter, at key 3, and the block is genuine Genesis 1 material - 'without form and void', the Spirit continuing to brood over it as a fowl does when hatching eggs - which belongs at v2. Every prior instance was a periodic run of donor-block text from another chapter or book at a fixed stride; this is a single block of the right chapter filed one verse late. Excluded from the 3-5 entry as misplaced.

Keil and Delitzsch chunking runs one entry ahead of the verse key throughout this chapter. Their block filed at a given verse consists of the running text of the next several verses followed by the opening of their section on the FOLLOWING day: v7 carries 'The Third Day', v10 'The Fourth Day', v15 'The Fifth Day', v21 'The Sixth Day'. The practical effect is that their comment on day N sits inside the entry covering day N-1. Usable at 9-13, where the fourth-day opening summarises the third day as a completed stage; excluded from 14-19, where the block carries no material on that span at all.

Basil the Great is the fifth confirmed voice under the 200-word hard cap (after Keil and Delitzsch, John Gill, Cyril of Jerusalem and John Lightfoot); every sampled block is exactly 200 words and several end mid-sentence. He is also the second voice hit by the scripts/synthesis_qa.py VOICE_LABELS gap: the list carries the bare string 'Basil', so _LABEL_RE never matches the header 'Basil the Great:', exactly as already recorded for 'Cyril' against 'Cyril of Jerusalem:'. Consequence is that a genuine Basil block cannot be named in excluded_voices without tripping the 'names a block absent from this entry's source' check, and his words are invisible to usable_source_words. Worked around here with a SILENT set that skips him in the ghost pass without ever emitting him into excluded_voices. The fix wants the long forms placed BEFORE the short ones in VOICE_LABELS, since alternation order decides the match, and it changes usable_source_words corpus-wide.

genesis 1 at 63,543 usable source words tiled into eight entries on Henry's own keying, which follows the days of creation: 1-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-13, 14-19, 20-25, 26-28, 29-31. Nine distinct voices in the chapter (Gill 31 verses, Ellicott 22, Clarke 19, Calvin 19, Keil and Delitzsch 11, Wesley 11, Henry 10, Basil the Great 9, Jamieson 1) with a maximum of eight on any single verse, so the 350-650 word window never bound on voice count here the way it does on NT chapters. Compare acts 2, where twelve voices keyed at verse 1 forced a single-verse entry. Further evidence that the picker's source-word budget mis-ranks OT against NT chapters: an OT chapter of 63,543 words took eight entries while an NT chapter of 117,188 took twelve.

The clearest statement of accommodation in the corpus so far stands at genesis 1:14-16, where Calvin defends the description of the moon as a great light: Moses does not descant as a philosopher on the secrets of nature but writes in a popular style what all persons of common sense can understand, while astronomers prove that Saturn is greater than the moon; the question is not how great the sun is but how much light comes to us; and astronomy itself is expressly not to be reprobated. Clarke reaches the same defence empirically, distinguishing bulk from light shed, while Gill goes the other way and supplies Derham's and Newton's measurements in the middle of a comment on the folly of worshipping the sun. At 1:26 the same three split again on the plural: Gill and Calvin take it of the Father addressing the Son and Spirit and reject the earth, the angels and the plural of majesty outright, while Ellicott records the Jewish readings and finds only the germ of the doctrine, expressly denying that it is a formal proof of the Trinity.

JFB donor residue confirmed for a fifth consecutive chapter, and again on the stride-6 pattern: vv.12/24/30 carry blocks belonging to 2 Kings 23 (sun-images) and to a Romans restoration passage, with nothing on the priestly dues of this chapter. The stride, not the content, remains the reliable detector — 1samuel 2 ran 5/11/17/23/29/35, numbers 5 ran 4/10/16/28, exodus 8 ran 10/22/28. JFB is excluded at entries 8, 20 and 25 on that ground.

Keil's only block inside span 8-19 (at v9) is a bare reprint of the AV text of vv.9-14 with no exposition attached. Excluded at entry 8 as note-425 Mode 2 (non-exposition), not as a trim casualty. Keil is genuinely used at entries 1, 20 and 25, so the voice is not absent from the chapter.

The ghost check caught a real omission this chapter, not a false positive: Gill had been trimmed out of entries 1 and 8 entirely, and Keil out of 8. Gill's blocks in both spans are short (13-71 words) but genuine exposition — the tribe of thy father as Amram's tribe, the Levites' concrete charge, not redeeming the firstlings meaning taking the creatures rather than a price — so note-425 Mode 1 applies and they were re-added, trading out an equal weight of Calvin and Wesley material already represented elsewhere in the same entries. Standing lesson: on a chapter that needs 10+ trim passes per entry, the last voice cited once is the one trimming will silently delete; run the ghost check before believing an entry is finished.

JFB donor residue again on the stride-6 lattice: vv.9, 15 and 27 carry Genesis 29-30 material (Sarah and Hagar, Leah adopting her maid's children, the rivalry of the two sisters, Leah's naming of her sons) with nothing on Dinah, Shechem or the massacre. Sixth consecutive chapter showing the pattern; the interval here is 9-15-27, i.e. the stride with one position skipped. JFB excluded at entries 6 and 25 on that ground.

Keil's blocks at v19 and v31 are bare AV reprints — v19 reprints vv.19-25 with no exposition attached, v31 is the single line of the verse and nothing more. Excluded at entries 18 and 30 as note-425 Mode 2. Keil is genuinely used at entries 1, 6 and 25, so the voice carries the chapter; the same defect appeared at numbers 18 v9 in this same batch, which suggests Keil's donor text drops into pure reprint at span boundaries rather than at random.

Henry files five whole-pericope overviews in this chapter (vv.1, 6, 18, 20, 25) and four of them mark the narrative seams exactly: 1-5 Dinah defiled, 6-17 the treaty and the deceitful condition, 18-24 the town persuaded, 25-31 massacre and rebuke. The chapter was sized to that reach and came out at five entries, splitting only Henry's last filing at 25-29 | 30-31 because its 6827 source words will not fit one entry (note 449). His fifth filing at v20 is a condensed duplicate of the v25 material, so it lands inside the 18-24 entry and was used there — its 'religion only pretended to' remark is in fact the right close for the entry about the town consenting for gain, which is the filing rule paying off rather than fighting the outline.

The sharpest disagreement in the chapter is over Dinah's own culpability, and it splits the corpus cleanly. Calvin holds that Moses in part casts the blame on her by recording that she went out; Henry and Wesley elaborate the same into a homily on gadding. Clarke flatly denies it, reading 'spake to the heart of the damsel' as evidence that there was no consent whatever, that the whole was violence, and that she was afterwards detained by force in Shechem's house until the sack. Recorded as a debate at entry 1 rather than resolved, since both readings are drawn from the same clause.

The strongest Jamieson residue pattern recorded so far. All seven Jamieson blocks in Luke 22 are foreign, and all come from Luke 11-12: v6 is the 'ask and it shall be given' cross-reference, v18 the finger of God against the Spirit of God, v30 the sign of Jonah, v36 the light of the body, v42 an illustration from familiar objects, v54 'Behold I send' from the woes on the scribes, v66 'my friends, there their power ends'. Six of the seven keys run at a stride of exactly 12 from offset 6 (6, 18, 30, 42, 54, 66), with one extra member at 36. Donor verses ascend monotonically with the target but not at a constant offset, so this is a compressed remapping of one donor passage across a longer target chapter rather than a fixed shift. Excluded from all seven entries.

Cyril of Alexandria's commentary is chunked exactly one pericope behind the verse key throughout this chapter, the cleanest systematic offset yet seen. Each block opens by quoting the text of the PREVIOUS section and then expounds it: the block at v7 covers 21:37-22:6, at v17 covers 22:7-16, at v24 covers 22:17-22, at v31 covers 22:24-30, at v35 covers 22:31-34, at v54 covers 22:47-53, at v63 covers 22:54-62. Seven instances with no exceptions. The practical effect for the loop is that his comment on a span is always found under the first key of the NEXT span, so an entry that cites him from its own key is usually citing him on the passage before. Handled here by using only what his block says that bears on the entry's own span, or by taking him from the Catena Aurea blocks labelled bare 'Cyril', which are correctly filed.

The catena blocks in this chapter are COMPOUND, which no previous chapter's tooling accounted for. The Name: header names only the FIRST father of a Catena Aurea run; every later father in the same block appears inline in capitals (GLOSS., BEDE;, CHRYS., THEOPHYL., TITUS BOST., AUG., AMBROSE;, GREG NYSS., DION. ALEX., EUSEBIUS., EPIPHAN.). Two consequences. First, the per-verse header list understates the voices actually present, so a ghost check run on headers alone is correct but a 'named but not sourced' check run on headers alone falsely rejects genuinely sourced fathers; the build script for this chapter therefore validates prose attributions against headers UNION inline labels while running the ghost pass on headers only, since requiring every inline father to be used is impossible at 650 words. Second, usable_source_words silently attributes every inline father's words to the header voice, so per-voice source measurement in catena books is wrong wherever these runs occur.

Pointer-only blocks are a defect class distinct from residue and should probably be named as such. Albert Barnes contributes nothing but bare cross-references on six of this chapter's fourteen spans ('Mt 26:17 Mt 26:18 Mk 14:12 ... Verse 7. (e) day of unleavened bread Ex 12:1 and following'), and John Wesley does the same on one. The block is genuinely about this passage, so it is not residue in the donor sense, but it carries no comment that can be cited, and a writer who names the voice anyway is inventing. Declared in excluded_voices here, which the validator accepts because the labels do occur in the blob; but the semantics recorded in synthesis_qa.py describe excluded_voices as residue, so either the documentation or the field wants widening.

Cyril of Jerusalem is the third voice hit by the scripts/synthesis_qa.py VOICE_LABELS gap, after Cyril of Alexandria and Basil the Great. The list carries the bare strings 'Cyril' and 'Basil', so _LABEL_RE, which requires the label to be followed by a colon, never matches the headers 'Cyril of Jerusalem:', 'Cyril of Alexandria:' or 'Basil the Great:'. That matters here because his blocks are relevant at some keys and pure foreign residue at others: at v20 he is on the table of the psalm and at v48 on the testimonies of the Passion, both apt, but at v55 he is on the firmament of Genesis 1, at v61 on 'rejoice in the Lord alway' and the voice crying in the wilderness, and at v69 on the sign of Jonah. Those three cannot be declared in excluded_voices without tripping the 'names a block absent from this entry's source' check, so they were skipped by a per-entry SILENT set instead. Three distinct labels for Cyril appear in this one chapter (Cyril, Cyril of Alexandria, Cyril of Jerusalem), the first two being the same father from two different sources. The fix remains to place the long forms BEFORE the short ones in VOICE_LABELS, since alternation order decides the match.

luke 22 at 63,923 usable source words and 71 verses took fourteen entries: 1-6, 7-13, 14-18, 19-20, 21-23, 24-30, 31-34, 35-38, 39-42, 43-46, 47, 48-53, 54-62, 63-71. Twenty-five distinct voice labels appear in the chapter, and the binding constraint throughout was voice count, not source words: the 31-34 entry carries fifteen sourced voices in 650 words, about forty-three words each, and verse 47 alone carries eleven and had to be its own entry. This is the third chapter in a row to show that the picker's source-word budget mis-ranks NT against OT chapters. Genesis 1 at 63,543 words - within 400 words of this chapter - took eight entries with a maximum of eight voices on any verse; luke 22 at 63,923 took fourteen with a maximum of fifteen. The two chapters are indistinguishable to the picker and roughly twice apart in the work they require. A voice-count term in the budget would separate them.

Two of the sharpest disagreements in the corpus so far stand in this chapter. At 22:21 the question is whether Judas received the Lord's Supper, and it turns entirely on where Luke places the exposure of the traitor: Lightfoot asks what more could be desired as a demonstration that he was present at the eucharist and dismisses the contrary argument from John 13 as making something out of nothing, Clarke reproduces that argument as his own, and Henry reaches the same conclusion from Luke placing the words after the institution where Matthew and Mark place them before; Wesley denies it flatly, since the sop belongs to a table already cleared before the bread and cup were brought, and Robertson records the difference of order without deciding. At 22:43 the question is what caused the agony: Wesley has Christ feeling the weight of the wrath of God surrounded by a host of devils, Gill a renewed and visible assault of Satan in a garden, while Lightfoot says outright that he dare not say or imagine that God was angry or conceived any indignation against him at all, and ascribes the bloody sweat to the bite of the old serpent, citing Diodorus on serpents whose bite brings an issue of sweat like blood.

JFB donor residue here is the cleanest instance of the stride-6 pattern yet found: vv.12, 18, 24, 30, 36 and 42 — six hits, unbroken, exactly six apart — every one of them Mark 9 / Matthew 18 material (the epileptic boy and his father, the little child set in the midst, 'let these sayings sink down into your ears'), with nothing whatever on the trial, the crucifixion or the burial. Seventh consecutive chapter showing the pattern. On this evidence the stride is a property of how the JFB donor text was sliced into the corpus, not a per-chapter accident, and a JFB block landing on a multiple-of-6 verse should be read as residue until proven otherwise. Excluded at entries 6, 15, 22, 27, 33 and 42.

Barnes and Wesley in this chapter are frequently not commentary at all but bare cross-reference stubs — Wesley 'Mt 27:1,2; Lu 22:66; Lu 23:1; John 18:28' at v1, Barnes '(l) "And when" Mt 27:45, Lk 23:44' at v33 and the same pattern at vv.34/36/37/40/41. Clarke's v1 block is the chapter argument (a verse-by-verse outline of all 47 verses) plus 'In the morning - See Mat 27:1'. All are note-425 Mode 2 and excluded where they are the voice's only content in a span: Clarke, Barnes and Wesley at entry 1, Barnes at entries 6, 33 and 38, Wesley at entry 27. Each of these voices is used normally elsewhere in the chapter, so the exclusions are local to the span, not to the chapter.

First NT chapter in this run, and the source shape differs materially from the OT books: mark 15 carries 16 top-level voices, not 10, adding A.T. Robertson, Albert Barnes and John Lightfoot alongside a patristic catena (Bede, Theophylact, Augustine, Pseudo-Jerome, Cyril of Jerusalem, the Gloss). The tags vocabulary differs too — luke 23, repaired 2026-08-18 under cow-prose-rules-2026-08-09 and the right model for a passion narrative, uses seven school slugs including latin-fathers and eastern-antiochene, and writes debates and outliers as FLAT STRINGS rather than the {question, sides} and {voice, claim} dicts the OT chapters use. Followed luke 23 exactly. School assignments taken from corpus practice: Robertson/Barnes/Lightfoot/JFB grammatical-historical, Bede/Augustine/Pseudo-Jerome/Gloss latin-fathers, Theophylact/Cyril of Jerusalem eastern-antiochene.

Two disagreements in this chapter are worth flagging as corpus-level, not local. (1) The crown of thorns: Clarke, following Bishop Pearce, argues the Greek word may derive from akanthos, the soft garden plant the French call branche ursine, cited as pliant by Virgil and Pliny and said to be common about Jerusalem — on which reading the crown was derision, not torture. Gill and Bede assume real thorns, Gill having them driven into the temples by the blow of the reed. Recorded as a debate at entry 15.
